boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.excerpt: The city says the U.S. Department of Transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors.
boston-roxbury-grant-lawsuit-2026.text: boston sues over $20m grant for roxbury street upgrades the city says the u.s. department of transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors. the city of boston has gone to federal court to recover a $20 million transportation grant that officials say was withdrawn after the project included a small electric-vehicle charging component. the lawsuit, filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of massachusetts, asks the court to reverse the u.s. department of transportation's cancellation of the 2022 award for the roxbury resilient corridors project. the filing and case number, city of boston v. duffy, are listed in the public docket record (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/massachusetts/madce/1:2026cv14419/306825). the dispute centers on three roxbury streets: melnea cass boulevard, malcolm x boulevard and warren street. boston's project page says the grant was intended to support street repairs, safer crossings, transit improvements, accessibility work, traffic-flow changes, trees, lighting, public spaces and stormwater features. the city describes the corridors as central roadways in a historically disinvested neighborhood and says the project was being developed with local residents and community organizations (https://www.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/roxbury-resilient-corridors). according to a sept. 28 announcement from u.s. rep. ayanna pressley and mayor michelle wu, the city argues that dot cited the project's electric-vehicle charging infrastructure as the reason for canceling the entire award. the announcement says that charging work represented less than 1% of project costs and that federal transportation officials had previously encouraged the city to include it. those are the city's allegations about the cancellation; the lawsuit has not produced a merits ruling (https://pressley.house.gov/2026/09/28/pressley-wu-announce-lawsuit-against-trump-administration-to-protect-20-million-federal-grant-for-roxburys-street-improvements/). the guardian independently reported that the case names transportation secretary sean duffy and was filed against the department over its decision to withdraw the money. the newspaper also reported the city's position that federal agencies cannot rewrite a program established by congress to match changing political priorities. the department's response was not included in the sources reviewed for this report, so the federal government's legal defense and any timetable for responding remain unclear (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/28/boston-sues-trump-administration). the stakes are practical for people who use roxbury's busiest routes. boston says the project is meant to improve bus service, walking, bicycling and driving conditions at the same time. on its warren street project page, the city says more than 20,250 mbta riders use that corridor each weekday and that delays can add as much as 20 minutes to an average rider's day. that page predates the lawsuit and describes the broader transit problem rather than measuring the effect of the canceled grant, but it helps explain why the city treats the award as more than a budget line (https://content.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/warren-street-bus-priority-corridor). roxbury's transportation history also shapes the argument. boston says the wide, vehicle-oriented corridors were created through eminent-domain and block-clearance decisions during the urban-renewal era of the 1960s. the city's current plan calls for safer crossings, more comfortable bus stops, shade and cooling spaces, bike infrastructure and green stormwater measures, while also trying to prevent displacement and support small businesses. those goals remain proposed project features, not completed improvements. the case arrives after the city had already approved accepting the federal award. a boston city council record from april 2025 describes the $20 million raise grant as funding to reconstruct and upgrade the three roxbury corridors. the city now says the cancellation removed a major share of the money needed to move the work forward. whether the court restores the award, sends the decision back to dot for reconsideration or leaves the cancellation in place will determine what boston can realistically build and when (https://content.boston.gov/departments/city-council/city-council-roll-call-votes?page=39). for now, the lawsuit is an opening filing, not a ruling that boston has won or that dot acted unlawfully. the public docket shows the case was assigned to u.s. district judge richard g. stearns after an initial judge recused himself on the filing date. the next meaningful developments will be the federal defendants' response, any request for interim relief and the court's decision on how the administrative procedure act claims proceed. until then, the three-corridor project remains listed by boston as pending, with its completion year undetermined. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston roxbury, boston massachusetts boston roxbury transportation federal grants public transit ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.excerpt: The season runs Oct. 3 through Oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission.
ct-fall-turkey-firearms-season-2026-10-0.text: connecticut fall firearms turkey season opens with updated permission rules the season runs oct. 3 through oct. 31, while a new state rule clarifies when small-game and turkey hunters need landowner permission. connecticut’s fall firearms turkey season opens saturday, oct. 3, and runs through oct. 31, the department of energy and environmental protection announced friday. the opening applies to eligible state and private lands, while the state’s pheasant and broader small-game seasons are scheduled to begin oct. 17. fall archery seasons for deer and turkey began sept. 15, giving connecticut hunters several overlapping ways to use the state’s forests and private landscapes this month. [deep’s opening notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/deep-announces-opening-days-of-fall-turkey-pheasant-and-small-game-hunting-seasons) describes the firearms opener as part of the agency’s annual schedule and urges hunters to participate safely and responsibly. the basic turkey rules are specific. the fall firearms bag limit is three turkeys of either sex on private land, state land or a combination of the two. hunting hours begin one-half hour before sunrise and end at sunset. connecticut residents need a firearms hunting license and a resident game bird conservation stamp. nonresidents need either a three-day out-of-state bird-hunting license or a nonresident firearms license, along with the stamp. the state’s [2026 wild-turkey guide](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/hunting/2026-connecticut-hunting-and-trapping-guide/wild-turkey-hunting) says shotguns must be 20 gauge or larger, use no. 4 through no. 7 1/2 shot or a permitted combination, and be limited to three shells. access rules matter as much as the season dates. a hunter on private land must carry signed written consent from the landowner on deep’s official form for the current season. turkey hunting is allowed on sundays only on private land, and sunday hunting cannot take place within 40 yards of a blazed public trail. hunters using state land should check deep’s interactive hunting-area map because not every state property is open to fall firearms turkey hunting. decoys are allowed, but live decoys are prohibited. the 2026 season also arrives with a permission change that took effect oct. 1. deep says verbal permission is sufficient for small-game hunting on private land every day of the week, including sundays. deer and turkey hunters still need written permission from private landowners. the agency also says the legal definition of a muzzleloader has changed: the projectile must be loaded from the muzzle end. those distinctions are important for people moving between small-game, deer and turkey seasons, because permission requirements do not apply identically to each activity. deep’s safety guidance focuses on preventing a person from being mistaken for a bird. hunters should remain in a fixed location and call turkeys to them rather than stalk a turkey or a turkey call. before firing, they should identify the target and what lies beyond it. the guide recommends sitting with protection from an approaching hunter, such as a tree at least as wide as the hunter’s shoulders, and placing a four- to six-inch fluorescent-orange band around the tree about six feet above the ground to identify the calling position. hunters should not wear red, white, blue or black while turkey hunting, and deep recommends fluorescent orange while walking to and from the hunting area and when carrying a harvested bird. harvest paperwork continues after a successful hunt. a hunter must immediately complete and sign a harvest tag and keep it with the turkey until the carcass is cut up for consumption. deep also requires deer and turkey harvests to be reported within 24 hours through its online hunter reporting website or by calling 1-877-337-4868, according to the agency’s [fall archery season notice](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/news-releases/news-releases---2026/fall-archery-deer-and-turkey-season-opens-in-september). the reporting requirement gives wildlife managers information for monitoring harvest and managing connecticut’s turkey population. for people sharing the woods, the opening changes the mix of activity on public properties beginning this weekend. hikers and other visitors should pay attention to posted notices and avoid entering closed or restricted areas, while hunters need to confirm the property rules before setting up. deep’s guide includes the season dates, license requirements, map links and landowner forms in one place. the next major statewide opening is oct. 17, when pheasant and several small-game seasons begin; closing dates vary by species. new-england new-england new england ct connecticut connecticut hunting season wild turkey outdoor safety deep

ct-i91-windsor-ejection-2026-10-01.text: person seriously injured after ejection in windsor i-91 crash a person was taken to hartford hospital with serious injuries after being ejected in a two-car crash that closed southbound i-91 in windsor thursday evening. one person was seriously injured thursday evening after being thrown from a vehicle in a two-car crash on interstate 91 south in windsor, connecticut state police said. the collision closed a section of the highway during the evening commute and remained under investigation overnight. connecticut department of transportation officials said the crash was reported at about 5:15 p.m. between exits 36 and 35b. the agency reported the southbound closure while state police and emergency crews worked at the scene. the reported closure covered both a windsor interchange and the adjoining southbound segment, making the incident a significant travel disruption for drivers using the corridor. state police told the connecticut post that the person ejected from the vehicle was taken to hartford hospital by windsor emergency medical services with serious injuries. authorities did not release the person's name, age or condition beyond that description. they also did not identify the other driver or disclose whether anyone else was hurt. multiple state police units responded, according to the connecticut post's account of the investigation. the newspaper reported that the scene was still active around 9:15 p.m., several hours after the crash was first reported. police had not announced a cause, and the available reports did not say whether speed, impairment, weather, a medical event or another factor played a role. those possibilities remain unconfirmed and should not be treated as explanations. the transportation disruption continued into the night. the connecticut post reported heavy traffic near the closure at about 9:23 p.m., citing the department of transportation. patch later reported that the highway reopened late thursday night. the closure limits reported by ctdot were the same in both accounts: southbound i-91 between exits 36 and 35b. patch reported early friday that windsor ems transported the injured person to hartford hospital and that connecticut state police were investigating. patch also noted that the reports did not identify the person or explain what caused the crash. wfsb, which first reported the closure, separately described the incident as a two-vehicle crash and attributed the road information to ctdot and the serious-injury information to state police. for windsor ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.excerpt: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.text: former connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to greece kosta diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him. former connecticut school-construction official konstantinos “kosta” diamantis was sentenced wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. the 70-year-old former state official had fled to greece before sentencing, and the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. the federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and. u.s. district judge stefan r. underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. a federal jury in bridgeport found diamantis guilty in october 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the justice department. connecticut public reported that the case grew out of diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the office of school construction grants and review. that office administered grants for connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. prosecutors said diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. the justice department identified projects involving a school project in tolland, state reimbursement work for new britain and renovations at hartford’s bulkeley high school. the release says one contractor paid diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations. the sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in september but did not attend. ct mirror reported that his lawyer told the court diamantis had left the united states and was in greece, where he holds dual citizenship. the later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the united states. the financial consequences are not settled. the justice department said judge underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. that decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. the unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court. the prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. ct mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. the difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue diamantis and the court addresses restitution. ct mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/. the case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. the justice department said contractors identified as duffy, monarca and roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. the investigation was conducted by the fbi and irs criminal investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. connecticut public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced. for connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. the court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved diamantis’s custody. those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors. new-england new-england new england ct bridgeport bridgeport, ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.text: connecticut awards $6.2m to 29 districts to improve student attendance the new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services. connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools. the grants, announced sept. 30 by gov. ned lamont and education commissioner charlene russell-tucker, are being distributed through the learner engagement and attendance program, known as leap. the money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. about $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program). leap pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. the visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. the program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. it later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year. the recipients include some of connecticut’s largest districts. waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, hartford $500,000, bridgeport $475,000 and new haven $425,000. stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including east windsor, east haven, plainfield and jamestown. middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide leap effort. state officials say connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. the governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. the figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that leap alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy. there is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. the center for connecticut education research collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and connecticut colleges, studied leap’s first 15 districts. its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. the study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort. connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since leap began. those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. the current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results. the immediate test will be local execution. districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. if the grants produce lasting attendance gains, connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut student attendance chronic absenteeism leap public schools education funding

ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.excerpt: A $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help Connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity.
ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.text: middletown veterans cemetery expansion will add 1,510 cremation plots a $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity. connecticut will expand the state veterans cemetery in middletown with 1,510 new burial plots for cremated remains, state officials announced friday. the project will use a $584,250 grant from the u.s. department of veterans affairs alongside $294,250 that connecticut has already allocated, adding capacity at a cemetery that serves veterans and eligible family members from across the state. the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-funding-to-expand-the-connecticut-state-veterans-cemetery-in-middletown) was also covered locally by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansion-add-cremation-burial-plots). the work is planned for a parcel next to the existing cemetery at 317 bow lane. the property was formerly used by connecticut valley hospital and was recently transferred from the state department of mental health and addiction services to the department of veterans affairs, which is overseeing the expansion. the location allows the state to extend an existing cemetery rather than wait for a separate site to be developed. under the state’s announcement, the federal money will pay for the cremains burial plots and related site work, including an entrance gate, fencing, landscaping, irrigation components, concrete-block storage bays, site furnishings and supporting infrastructure. the state funding will support demolition of cottage 22, a vacant connecticut valley hospital building on the property. connecticut has not announced a completion date for the construction. the expansion is aimed at a specific capacity problem. the [connecticut department of veterans affairs](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the middletown cemetery currently has 14,718 burial plots and 3,000 columbarium niches. state officials estimate that the existing supply of in-ground cremation plots will be exhausted around january 2028 without additional space; with the expansion, those plots are projected to remain available through at least december 2033. that timing matters because the cemetery offers several distinct choices for families. the project concerns in-ground burial of cremated remains, while casket burials and above-ground columbarium niches are separate options. the state says extending the cremation-plot supply through 2033 would bring the estimated depletion dates for all three options into alignment, giving officials time to plan a future cemetery intended to serve veterans and their families over the longer term. the middletown site was established in 1985 and is the largest state-operated veterans cemetery in connecticut, according to the department of veterans affairs. the department’s [cemetery-services page](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the site is the final resting place for more than 16,000 veterans and family members. connecticut also maintains the colonel raymond f. gates cemetery in rocky hill, which is reserved primarily for veterans residing at the state’s residential and skilled-nursing facilities, and provides perpetual care for spring grove veterans cemetery in darien, which is closed to new burials. the funding announcement follows a longer state effort to secure land and keep the middletown facility eligible for federal cemetery support. a [2023 state bond authorization](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/opm/bud-capital-budget/agendas/cy-2023/agenda%5fdec15%5f2023.pdf) set aside $3 million for land acquisition and improvements connected to the department of veterans affairs cemetery program. a subsequent state planning document said the middletown cemetery was expected to approach capacity within several years, while an [environmental scoping notice](https://portal.ct.gov/ceq/das/scoping-notice/dva-cemetery-expansion) identified the bow lane expansion area and estimated that existing space could be depleted in about 4.6 years. for connecticut veterans’ families, the immediate result is a planned increase in local burial capacity, not a new benefit or completed construction project. the state and federal awards still have to be translated into demolition, site preparation and cemetery improvements. the announcement does not specify the construction schedule or the final operating date for the new plots. the department of veterans affairs will remain responsible for project oversight and for coordinating burial services while the expansion proceeds. connecticut veterans veterans ct middletown middletown, connecticut connecticut middletown veterans cemeteries department of veterans affairs

ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.excerpt: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.text: connecticut awards $10.5m for 50 recreational-trail projects the grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities. connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, gov. ned lamont and the department of energy and environmental protection announced thursday. the awards come through the connecticut recreational trails grant program after a competitive review by deep and the connecticut greenways council. the money was previously allocated by the state bond commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). the program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance. that mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the sue grossman still river greenway. new haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the east rock park college woods inclusive community trail, while naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the naugatuck river greenway between naugatuck and waterbury. bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the old mill green pathways project, and east hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the east coast greenway. the geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at steep rock association’s hidden valley preserve, $492,874 for the university of connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the connecticut forest and park association’s blue-blazed trail system and woodland conservation corps. the full award table also includes projects in eastern connecticut, the shoreline, the hartford region and the northwest hills. twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. that designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. the state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections. there is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. connecticut’s trail census, a uconn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. the [uconn ct trails program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total. the program also arrives as connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. deep describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round. the next phase will be local implementation. planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. for residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. the grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut recreational trails deep outdoor recreation public access infrastructure

ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.excerpt: A Region 12 bus carrying students left South Grand Street and struck a building Thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation.
ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.text: suffield school bus crash sends 11 to hospitals with minor injuries a region 12 bus carrying students left south grand street and struck a building thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation. eleven people were taken to two local hospitals with minor injuries thursday after a small school bus carrying students left the roadway and struck a building in suffield, connecticut. the crash brought police, fire and ambulance crews to south grand street and left investigators working to determine why the bus veered off the road. suffield police said officers responded to the area of 425 south grand st. at about 9:49 a.m. after receiving a report of a motor-vehicle crash with possible injuries. their preliminary account said the bus was traveling north toward mountain road when it left the right shoulder and collided with a building beside the street. police did not announce a mechanical problem, medical event, weather factor or other cause. the bus came from regional school district 12, which serves communities in the shepaug valley. nbc connecticut reported that students were aboard, while the suffield concerns about campus safety. his request would bar uconn from disconnecting, disabling, removing or decommissioning the existing blue-light phones and associated safety lights at storrs while the ma-blandford-wildlife-corridor-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts protects 580 acres in blandford wildlife corridor the new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the mass. pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western massachusetts. massachusetts conservation agencies and the nature conservancy have completed a project protecting more than 580 acres in blandford, creating new public land on both sides of interstate 90 and strengthening a wildlife connection through the western massachusetts hills. the [massachusetts executive office of energy and environmental affairs](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-protects-over-580-acres-for-wildlife-and-outdoor-recreation-in-blandford) announced the project oct. 2. [western mass news](https://www.westernmassnews.com/2026/10/03/more-land-added-chester-blandford-stare-forest/) independently reported the same acreage and the new designations. the protected property is divided into a 360-acre masswildlife blandford wildlife management area and a 218-acre addition to chester-blandford state forest. the former christmas tree farm crosses the mass. pike and connects more than 39,000 acres of already protected land, according to state officials and the local report. that makes the project more than a stand-alone open-space purchase: it closes a gap in a larger landscape where animals can move between habitat on opposite sides of one of new england's busiest highways. the land is open to the public for outdoor recreation, although the announcement did not provide a separate trail map, parking plan or operating schedule for the new management area. residents and visitors will need to rely on updates from masswildlife and the department of conservation and recreation for practical access information as management details are posted. the property contains mature and young forest, agricultural grasslands, wetlands and four brooks: sanderson, cushman, finley and peebles. those waterways are part of the westfield river watershed. state agencies said the conservation work will help protect water quality and nearby drinking-water supplies, while preserving cold-water fish habitat used by species such as eastern brook trout. the corridor also has a direct transportation-safety dimension. the state says masswildlife, dcr, massdot and the nature conservancy have been working to understand how animals cross roads and highways. at the blandford site, massdot and the nature conservancy are monitoring a culvert under i-90, where black bears, bobcats, coyotes, river otters and other wildlife have been documented passing through, according to the state announcement. keeping that route connected can help animals reach food, water and seasonal habitat while giving planners evidence for future crossing improvements. the project includes habitat that can support the new england cottontail, massachusetts' only native rabbit, which state officials describe as vulnerable to habitat loss. protecting connected forest and grassland does not guarantee that the rabbit or any other species will expand here, but it preserves the kind of varied landscape wildlife managers say is necessary for movement and adaptation as conditions change. blandford's acquisition is part of a broader state conservation strategy. massachusetts' biodiversity goals call for doubling the pace of land and water protection, with targets of conserving 30 percent by 2030 and 40 percent by 2050. the administration said its proposed mass ready act includes $304.5 million for land-protection programs and $20 million tied to biodiversity goals; those are proposed investments, not funds this project alone received. for the hilltowns, the immediate result is a permanently protected stretch of forest, streams and open land that can serve both residents and wildlife. the agencies involved still have to translate the acquisition into day-to-day public access and long-term habitat management. the new designations give them the protected footprint; future agency plans will determine how visitors use it and how the corridor is monitored over ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.excerpt: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. the proposed timing was described by outgoing department of higher education commissioner noe ortega during the board of higher education's sept. 29 meeting, according to wbur and the state house news service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools). the change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. under the state's financial assessment and risk monitoring, or farm, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. the massachusetts department of higher education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp). the state already requires colleges to alert the board of higher education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. the department's farm materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. the department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites. the proposed dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. wbur reported that current regulations use dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. board chairman chris gabrieli said a december determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester. the discussion follows two massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, wbur reported. hampshire's public notice from the department of higher education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-hampshire-noitce-posting-for-dhe-website.pdf). the notice also says the department could not confirm that hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every massachusetts college faces the same condition. massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of mount ida college. the department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 farm law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. the department's current process describes screening from november through april, review of risk-mitigation plans from june through october, and determinations and contingency planning in november and december. officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. the goal, gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. the timing matters this fall because ortega's term as commissioner ended sept. 30 and josé luis santos began serving as interim commissioner on oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/). the public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. the next questions are whether the board of higher education formally adopts the dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual farm review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students. massachusetts massachusetts very poor keeping-quality forecast. the warning does not by itself predict the size of the harvest or say that every bog will be affected in the same way. it does mean growers and buyers are entering farms in wareham, where the massachusetts department of agricultural resources gathered with growers and local officials to mark the start of the harvest. the department says massachusetts has about ma-great-barrington-housatonic-water-eme.text: great barrington races to keep housatonic water flowing as emergency link remains unresolved the town says an emergency connection is supporting housatonic water works while state regulators require a continuous-service agreement, leaving customers facing a bottled-water contingency and a longer fight over the system’s future. great barrington officials are working to keep water service running for customers of housatonic water works while the private utility, the great barrington fire district and state regulators try to resolve the status of an emergency connection. in an oct. 1 public statement, the town said the temporary connection is supporting the hww system, but continued use requires an agreement for continuous service between fire district to keep supplying hww through the temporary link. massdep will not approve continued use until hww and the fire district reach an agreement and hww incorporates that agreement into its switched to bottled-water distribution. the town said it is coordinating with massdep on logistical planning in case an interruption occurs and would assist state agencies if residents need help. the immediate problem sits on top of a longer-running water-quality dispute in housatonic village, a great barrington community. wamc reported in september, citing an interview with berkshire eagle reporter talia lissauer, that excess manganese has caused water discoloration ranging from yellow to a dark coffee color and affects about 800 people. lissauer said she was aware of no health impacts from the discoloration, but residents have continued to seek a durable fix. the [wamc report](https://www.wamc.org/news/2026-09-03/mass-utility-company-faces-scrutiny-residents-face-chronic-issues-with-discolored-water) also described roughly 16 miles of aging pipe that ultimately need replacement. massdep has already penalized hww for missing a treatment deadline. the agency said in june that a july 2025 consent order required a manganese treatment plant at the great barrington would continue tracking compliance. the town is pursuing a separate long-term path through the massachusetts department of public utilities. great barrington and hww jointly filed a petition seeking a 1 update said the valuation proceeding remains active and that the town is communicating with the dpu, the attorney general’s office and state officials about a sustainable solution. residents have page](https://www.townofgbma.gov/371/housatonic-water-works-information-resou). the program does not resolve the utility’s infrastructure problems, but it recognizes costs residents have incurred officials must address the unfinished treatment plant, aging distribution lines and the pending valuation process. great barrington said it will post additional updates as information can be released. ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.text: massachusetts awards nearly $40m in life-science tax incentives tied to 1,644 jobs the awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside boston and cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting. massachusetts has awarded nearly $40 million in tax incentives to 38 life-science companies that collectively pledged to create 1,644 new jobs, putting a statewide economic-development program behind expansions in research, therapeutics, diagnostics and manufacturing. gov. maura healey announced the awards sept. 28 at smc ltd. in devens. the figures describe company commitments, not jobs already filled or money paid directly to workers. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the geographic distribution is a central feature of this round. the massachusetts life sciences center said 31 of the 38 awardees are expanding outside boston and cambridge, and those projects account for 71% of the expected new jobs. that puts communities such as acton, andover, bedford, burlington, chelmsford, devens, framingham, marlborough, milford, northbridge, sudbury, waltham and woburn in the direct path of the announced hiring commitments, rather than limiting the benefit to the state's traditional laboratory hubs. the agency described the program as a way to use massachusetts' broader network of life-science assets for growth and retention. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the largest individual award goes to acton-based insulet corporation: $10 million tied to a 250-job commitment. lila sciences in cambridge received $3.6 million for 200 jobs, while vertex pharmaceuticals in boston received $3.025 million for 121 jobs. other sizable awards include $2.875 million for bristol myers squibb's 125-job commitment in devens, $1.86 million for transmedics in andover, and $1.35 million for smc's 54 jobs in devens. the boston business journal reported that the full list also includes astrazeneca, vericel, zoll medical, rentschler biopharma and dozens of smaller firms. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the awards are tax incentives administered through the massachusetts life sciences center's tax incentive program jointly with the department of revenue. the program is open to companies doing research and development, commercialization or manufacturing in massachusetts, and the commitments are meant to be new, long-term positions. awardees must maintain their job commitments for three years and file regular reports documenting the jobs created as a result of the incentives. that structure makes the announced 1,644 jobs a measurable target that can be checked over time, rather than an immediate headcount. the state release also says the program has supported commitments for more than 22,300 jobs since the center was established. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) demand for the program was stronger than the award total. the boston business journal reported that companies submitted $58 million in applications this year, compared with a previous year when the center needed two rounds to allocate the full $40 million authorization. the outlet also reported that, since 2009, the center has made 519 awards to nearly 300 distinct companies totaling about $422 million and tied to more than 22,300 jobs. those figures show both the scale of the state's strategy and the competitive choices behind this year's list: the program is not an open-ended subsidy for every applicant, and some proposals were not funded in this cycle. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the current ceiling comes from the 2024 mass leads act, which raised the annual statutory cap for life-science tax incentives from $30 million to $40 million and broadened the eligible field to include areas such as medical technology, preventative medicine, biosecurity and life-science-related artificial intelligence. massachusetts' technical tax guidance describes the program as a collection of tax incentives available to qualifying companies, rather than a single grant pot. that distinction matters when evaluating the public return: the state is trading foregone tax revenue for promised hiring and investment, while the companies still have to execute their expansion plans. (https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-25-5-tax-provisions-in-certain-massachusetts-legislation-enacted-in-2024) for workers and municipalities, the next test is delivery. companies must meet the hiring and retention conditions attached to their awards, and the state must report whether projects translate into sustained employment across the commonwealth. the announcement includes activity in artificial intelligence, women's health, therapeutics, diagnostics, medical technology, research and development and biomanufacturing. if the commitments hold, the round will distribute new positions across a wider geography and reinforce massachusetts' life-science supply chain; if projects fall short, the reporting and tax-administration process will determine how the state responds. the award announcement establishes the targets, but future compliance records will show how many jobs actually materialize. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma massachusetts massachusetts life sciences tax incentives jobs economic development biotechnology

ma-masshealth-immigrant-coverage-2026-10.excerpt: A federal eligibility change taking effect Oct. 1 moves some lawfully present immigrants from full MassHealth coverage to narrower programs, while others remain eligible for comprehensive care.
ma-masshealth-immigrant-coverage-2026-10.text: masshealth coverage changes reach 7,300 immigrants in massachusetts a federal eligibility change taking effect oct. 1 moves some lawfully present immigrants from full masshealth coverage to narrower programs, while others remain eligible for comprehensive care. a federal eligibility change took effect thursday for about 7,300 massachusetts residents who are lawfully present immigrants and receive masshealth, the state’s medicaid program. the change does not apply to u.s. citizens or nationals, and it does not end coverage for every immigrant in the affected legal categories. it changes which federal and state-funded coverage programs are available to particular members based on immigration status, age, pregnancy, disability and other eligibility factors, according to the [masshealth information page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masshealth-information-for-noncitizens) and a september eligibility memo to state staff. the affected groups can include refugees, people granted asylum, some humanitarian parolees, certain survivors of abuse or trafficking and other categories that federal law previously treated as eligible for comprehensive medicaid. masshealth estimates that approximately 7,300 members are affected in massachusetts. the [boston globe reported](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/29/metro/masshealth-medicaid-immigrants-refugees/) that more than 8,000 additional people in connecticut, maine, new hampshire, rhode island and vermont are expected to lose comprehensive coverage in the same federal change, putting the massachusetts shift inside a wider new england disruption. the practical result will not be identical for everyone. children younger than 21 and people who are pregnant or postpartum generally keep their prior comprehensive coverage under the state’s guidance. older adults and disabled adults who meet income and asset rules can generally move to masshealth family assistance, which continues to provide comprehensive coverage but has different program rules. some other adults will move to masshealth limited and the health safety net, programs that can help pay for emergency services or medically necessary care at participating hospitals and community health centers but do not replace the full range of masshealth standard benefits. the [gbh report](https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-09-21/health-advocates-warn-of-masshealth-changes-for-immigrants-coming-oct-1) described the change as a loss of full standard or care plus coverage for certain immigrants. health advocates told gbh that some members will be moved to family assistance while others will have only masshealth limited and health safety net coverage. the distinction matters at the point of care: a narrower program may help with an emergency or a qualifying visit without covering routine primary care, most prescriptions, dental care, vision care or long-term services in the same way as comprehensive coverage. masshealth and community organizations have been notifying members in stages. health care for all told gbh that notices went to roughly 2,000 people in june and more than 5,000 in july and august, followed by final notices explaining the member’s new status and appeal rights. the state’s public guidance says affected members should review their notices, respond to requests for information and use the state’s screening and assistance resources rather than assume that an immigration-status change affects everyone in the same way. the change is likely to be felt most heavily in the state’s immigrant-serving health and social-service networks. health care for all identified suffolk, middlesex, essex and worcester counties as having the largest shares of affected immigrants covered through connectorcare, with spanish, brazilian portuguese, haitian creole, chinese and russian among the languages spoken by people receiving outreach. those county and language figures describe where advocates expect communication needs, not a count of every affected masshealth member. the immediate coverage change also arrives before a second phase of federal medicaid changes. masshealth says some adults ages 19 through 64 will face new work or education reporting requirements and more frequent renewals beginning in january 2027. massachusetts has launched a statewide campaign with health care for all and community organizations to help members understand those rules, but the state must implement the federal requirements while trying to limit avoidable coverage losses. for massachusetts residents, the next step is individual rather than political: check the notice from masshealth, confirm which program is listed, and ask for help if the decision appears to overlook age, pregnancy, disability, income or immigration documents. the state’s published rules make clear that being lawfully present is not itself a guarantee of one particular masshealth category, but neither does the oct. 1 change mean that all immigrants lose health coverage. the outcome depends on the member’s full eligibility record and on whether the person uses the appeal process when the state’s determination is disputed. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts masshealth medicaid ma-nantucket-missing-medical-plane-2026-.excerpt: A Canadian-registered air ambulance lost contact with federal flight controllers early Saturday while traveling from Bermuda to Boston, prompting an air-and-sea search south of Nantucket.
ma-nantucket-missing-medical-plane-2026-.text: coast guard searches off nantucket for missing medical plane with six aboard a canadian-registered air ambulance lost contact with federal flight controllers early saturday while traveling from bermuda to boston, prompting an air-and-sea search south of nantucket. the u.s. coast guard is searching waters off nantucket for a medical transport aircraft that lost contact with federal flight controllers early saturday while flying from bermuda to boston. the coast guard’s northeast district said in an [official update](https://x.com/uscgnortheast/status/2106332164568801317) that the gulfstream g100 had six people aboard and that air and surface crews had begun looking for it. the federal aviation administration confirmed to [boston 25 news](https://www.boston25news.com/news/local/coast-guard-searching-missing-medical-transfer-jet-bound-boston/dlhufcdj2fcmbesr4w3miioefa/) that it had lost contact with the flight. the aircraft departed l.f. wade international airport in bermuda on a flight to boston logan international airport. the faa issued a search-and-rescue alert at about 1:20 a.m. saturday, according to [cbs news](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/medical-plane-missing-nantucket-six-on-board/). cbs reported that the jet took off at about 11:40 p.m. eastern time friday and was expected to reach logan at roughly 1:30 a.m. the plane did not arrive, massachusetts port authority spokesperson jennifer mehigan told boston 25, which said the search area was off nantucket. the aircraft was identified as a gulfstream g-100 with canadian registration c-grjp. boston 25 reported that it is operated by latitude air ambulance, an ontario-based company that provides medical transfers. the associated press said the canadian-registered jet had four crew members and two passengers when it left bermuda. officials have not released the names, ages or medical circumstances of anyone aboard, and those details should not be inferred from the aircraft’s role as an air ambulance. the response is drawing resources from across the region. boston 25 reported that the coast guard deployed an hc-144 ocean sentry aircraft and an mh-60 jayhawk helicopter from air station cape cod, a 47-foot motor lifeboat crew from station brant point on nantucket and the coast guard cutter william sparling. [npr reported](https://www.npr.org/2026/10/03/nx-s1-5597878/coast-guard-searching-for-missing-medical-plane-carrying-6-people) that the agency also sent an hc-130 hercules aircraft. the mix of aircraft, boats and a cutter reflects the size of the ocean search area and the need to look from the air and the water. local authorities are involved as the search extends beyond the federal crews. the [martha’s vineyard times](https://www.mvtimes.com/2026/10/03/coast-guard-searching-for-missing-plane-off-nantucket/) reported that nantucket memorial airport manager preston harimon said the aircraft had reportedly declared an emergency before contact was lost. the airport manager said coast guard-led rescue work was underway, while nantucket police and harbormaster personnel were searching along the island’s south shore. that account adds a ground-and-shore component to a case centered offshore. the last known circumstances remain incomplete. the associated press reported that air-traffic-control audio captured a controller asking whether the pilot was “coming in blind,” then confirming that the pilot had declared an emergency before the communication ended. the pilot’s words were not audible in the recording, and the audio does not establish what caused the emergency. flight-tracking data reviewed by cbs showed a rapid descent before contact was lost, but that data alone does not explain the aircraft’s condition or location. the search also has an international dimension. ap reported that four of the six people aboard were canadian nationals and that canada’s transport minister said his government was monitoring the response. bermuda airport operator skyport told ap that the aircraft had four crew members and two passengers. bermuda premier david burt said, according to cbs, that officials were in contact with families and were hoping all six people would be found safe. as of the latest agency and public-broadcaster reports reviewed saturday evening, the coast guard had not announced that the plane or any person aboard had been found. the coast guard said it would provide updates as they became available, while the national transportation safety board told ap it was gathering information and had no further update at the time of that report. for nantucket, cape cod and boston, the immediate confirmed story is an active search in nearby waters—not a confirmed crash sequence, casualty count or cause. those questions remain for investigators and rescuers to establish. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma nantucket nantucket, ma-one-stop-growth-awards-2026-10-02.excerpt: The largest Community One Stop for Growth round to date is expected to support more than 27,000 homes and 13,000 permanent jobs, with South Coast communities receiving $6.5 million for housing, infrastructure and downtown reuse.
ma-one-stop-growth-awards-2026-10-02.text: massachusetts awards $330m for housing and local growth projects the largest community one stop for growth round to date is expected to support more than 27,000 homes and 13,000 permanent jobs, with south coast communities receiving $6.5 million for housing, infrastructure and downtown reuse. massachusetts is directing $330 million to 403 housing and economic-development projects in 207 communities, the healey administration announced oct. 1. state officials say the fiscal 2027 community one stop for growth awards are the largest single round in the program's history and are expected to support more than 27,000 new homes, more than 13,000 permanent jobs and more than 7 million square feet of commercial development. the administration also estimates that the projects could help unlock $24.6 billion in private investment. those are projected results, not homes or jobs already delivered. the awards are designed to help cities, towns and other organizations move projects from planning to construction or reuse. the state describes the community one stop for growth as a coordinated application and review process for housing and economic-development programs, rather than a single construction grant. the current awards are being administered through 14 programs involving the executive office of economic development, the executive office of housing and livable communities, and massdevelopment, according to the massachusetts municipal association's account of the announcement. the state's program overview is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth. the largest portions of the round are aimed at infrastructure that can make development possible. the massachusetts municipal association reported $109.7 million for 54 housingworks infrastructure projects, $105.1 million for 59 massworks projects and $51.1 million for 24 mbta community catalyst fund projects. other awards cover underused properties, seaport-related work, rural development, downtown improvements, site readiness, planning and brownfield redevelopment. the mix matters because a housing proposal can stall for reasons that are not solved by building financing alone, including streets, utilities, site cleanup and public-space improvements. the geographic reach is also part of the administration's case for the program. the awards extend to every region of massachusetts, and the municipal association said 13 communities are receiving one stop funding for the first time. the administration's breakdown, as reported by the association, puts 36% of projects in rural communities, 24% in gateway cities, 37% in housing choice communities and about half in mbta communities. that distribution describes the locations of awarded projects; it does not guarantee that each community will produce the number of homes or jobs projected for the statewide round. on the south coast, new bedford-area communities are set to receive $6.5 million, according to new bedford guide. new bedford's share totals $4,079,800, including $600,000 for repairs and life-safety upgrades at the star store in the downtown arts district. the work is intended to help artists and creative developers reoccupy the building as it moves toward a planned 2027 reopening. another $900,000 will support the conversion of a vacant former nursing home on acushnet avenue into dozens of workforce-housing units, while other awards address riverside development, waterfront and downtown lighting, and public-safety infrastructure. the local report is at https://www.newbedfordguide.com/6-5-million-awarded-economic-development-grants-new-bedford-senate-district/2026/10/01. dartmouth is slated to receive $2.265 million, most of it for sewer-pump improvements and replacements intended to add capacity for new housing, new bedford guide reported. a smaller dartmouth award will study potential uses for a former police station. fairhaven will use funding for improvements around the pease park boating area, including stormwater work and public amenities, while mattapoisett will develop standards for its village business district. those local examples show how the statewide program combines housing production with the less visible infrastructure and planning work that supports it. the massachusetts municipal association, which represents the state's cities and towns, said local governments often lack the resources to take on projects of this scale without state partnerships. that is an advocacy group's assessment, not an independent evaluation of the awards' economic return. for residents, the practical test will be whether the money leads to completed infrastructure, occupied homes, reopened commercial space and sustained employment rather than remaining at the announcement stage. the state says the full list of recipients and project descriptions is available through its community one stop for growth awards dashboard at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/community-one-stop-for-growth-awards. the program schedule says contracting is expected to begin in november 2026. project timing will vary by municipality and grant program, so the next milestones are contracting, local approvals and construction or reuse work. the oct. 1 announcement establishes the awards and their projected benefits; later records will show which projects advance and which targets are ultimately met. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts housing ma-opportunity-zones-2026-10-02.excerpt: The proposed federal tax-incentive areas would take effect in 2027, but Treasury certification and private investment decisions are still ahead.
ma-opportunity-zones-2026-10-02.text: massachusetts nominates 104 opportunity zones across 46 municipalities the proposed federal tax-incentive areas would take effect in 2027, but treasury certification and private investment decisions are still ahead. massachusetts has nominated 104 census tracts in 46 municipalities for the next round of federal opportunity zone designations, opening a new phase in the state’s effort to steer private investment toward neighborhoods with housing, business and infrastructure needs. the healey-driscoll administration submitted the nominations to the u.s. department of the treasury on oct. 2, according to the [state’s 2026 opportunity zone program page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/2026-massachusetts-opportunity-zone-program). the nomination is not the same as a final federal designation. treasury still has to review and certify the tracts, and the state says that decision is expected later this fall. if the nominations are certified, the new zones will take effect jan. 1, 2027, and remain in place through dec. 31, 2036. until that review is complete, communities and investors do not have a final map to rely on. the scale is limited by the updated federal rules. massachusetts had 414 eligible tracts to choose from but could nominate no more than 104, or roughly one-quarter of that pool. the state says the new eligibility standards are stricter than the rules used for the 2018 round, when 138 massachusetts tracts were designated. a tract generally had to have a median family income at or below 70% of the area median, or a poverty rate of at least 20% combined with a median family income no higher than 125% of the area median. contiguous tracts that might previously have been grouped together are no longer eligible under the updated rules, the state says. the proposed map reaches several different parts of the massachusetts economy. the state highlights innovation districts in amherst, boston, cambridge, lowell and worcester, where universities and research institutions are tied to early-stage companies. it also points to working waterfronts from new bedford to gloucester, public-housing revitalization in boston, and more than a dozen mbta communities districts, including fall river, framingham and haverhill. in smaller central and western massachusetts hubs, the state identifies athol, gardner, greenfield, montague, north adams and southbridge as places where mixed-use development could benefit from the designation. opportunity zones work through federal tax treatment rather than a direct state construction grant. the [u.s. treasury](https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/tax-policy/data-transparency/qualified-opportunity-zones) says taxpayers who make qualifying investments in designated census tracts through qualified opportunity funds may be eligible for tax benefits under section 1400z-2 of the internal revenue code. the state’s [frequently asked questions](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/frequently-asked-opportunity-zone-questions) likewise explains that a designation makes investments eligible for incentives but does not itself attract money or guarantee that a project will be built. communities still have to market sites, align zoning and permitting, and persuade investors that a project can work. the 2026 framework includes enhanced treatment for rural funds. the state says a qualified rural opportunity fund investing in rural opportunity zones can use a 50% substantial-improvement threshold, compared with 100% elsewhere, and can receive a 30% basis step-up after five years instead of the 10% step-up available to other funds. those provisions are intended to account for the different financing conditions in rural areas, but they do not predict how much capital will reach any particular town. the immediate next step is federal certification, followed by local and private-sector decisions about which sites are ready for investment. massachusetts says its selection process considered project readiness, local support, zoning and other public investments, but the nomination page does not promise a dollar amount, construction schedule or job total for any municipality. the practical test will come after the map is final: whether the tax incentive helps produce or preserve housing, strengthen small-city and rural economies, and move long-planned projects from eligibility to construction. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma massachusetts massachusetts opportunity zones economic development
