ma-project-rare-gas-pipeline-review-2026.excerpt: Project RARE would replace and add sections of Enbridge's Algonquin system in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, a proposal supporters tie to winter energy costs and critics say would prolong fossil-fuel dependence.
ma-project-rare-gas-pipeline-review-2026.text: healey urges faster federal review of new england gas pipeline expansion project rare would replace and add sections of enbridge's algonquin system in massachusetts and rhode island, a proposal supporters tie to winter energy costs and critics say would prolong fossil-fuel dependence. massachusetts gov. maura healey is asking the federal government to move faster on its review of a proposed natural-gas pipeline expansion that would reach into massachusetts and rhode island. in a letter to u.s. energy secretary chris wright, healey said the reliable affordable resilient enhancement project, known as project rare, could lower costs for about 600,000 customers. her request does not approve the project: federal regulators are still in the pre-filing environmental-review stage. the governor's letter is the latest turn in a regional argument over how to handle new england's high winter energy costs. healey's administration says constrained gas supply on the coldest days can push power plants toward more expensive oil and force utilities to buy liquefied natural gas. the administration is asking for a timely review while saying environmental review and community engagement should continue. the massachusetts announcement is at https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-calls-on-trump-administration-to-expedite-review-of-gas-pipeline-expansion. project rare is being developed by enbridge along its algonquin natural-gas system, which runs from new jersey through new york and southern new england. wbur reported that the proposal would replace about eight miles of existing pipe with larger-diameter pipe in massachusetts and rhode island, add a parallel section in rhode island and upgrade a compressor station in cromwell, connecticut. enbridge has said the expansion would add roughly 75 million cubic feet per day of capacity. wbur's report is at https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/01/governor-healey-project-rare-natural-gas-pipeline-expansion-fossil-fuels-climate. federal records provide a more detailed picture of the footprint. the federal energy regulatory commission says the planned facilities total about 13.5 miles in massachusetts and rhode island. the proposal includes replacing about 8.25 miles of 16-inch pipe with 36-inch pipe in norfolk and worcester counties and providence county, rhode island; installing about 2.2 miles of 12-inch looping pipe in newport county; and adding three miles of 36-inch looping pipe in providence county. it also includes software-related compression changes at the cromwell station. ferc's project page, docket pf26-7-000, says the project has not been approved: https://www.ferc.gov/algonquin-gas-transmission-enhancement-project. the local stakes extend beyond a construction map. ferc says the project is intended to increase supply to local distribution companies and improve regional reliability, while the massachusetts administration and eversource have connected new capacity to lower winter reliance on liquefied natural gas. wbur reported that massachusetts regulators approved a 10-year eversource purchase plan tied to the expansion and that the state estimates it could reduce the utility's liquefied-natural-gas use by about $40 million annually. that estimate is a projected benefit, not a guaranteed reduction on a household bill. the project is also colliding with massachusetts' climate requirements and a broader fight over the role of gas in the regional grid. wbur reported that climate advocates questioned whether adding pipeline capacity could lock in more gas use even if it reduces short-term reliance on liquefied natural gas. conservation law foundation said healey's request repeated a claim about lower heating costs that the group disputes, arguing that cleaner hydroelectric and offshore-wind deliveries have been the more reliable source of price containment. clf's response is at https://www.clf.org/newsroom/clf-challenges-gas-pipeline-push/. ferc's pre-filing process is not the final permitting decision. the agency describes it as a pre-application phase designed to surface environmental issues before an official application, with opportunities for public comments, open houses and scoping sessions. that means residents, landowners and communities along the proposed work areas still have a formal role as the record develops. the agency's page lists earlier 2026 open houses in wrentham and bellingham, massachusetts, and in several rhode island communities; later filings and notices will determine the next steps. for massachusetts, the immediate question is whether faster federal attention produces a faster decision without narrowing the review. healey is positioning project rare as one response to costly winter energy constraints, while environmental groups warn that the long-term answer must reduce dependence on fossil fuels. until enbridge files the project for full federal review and regulators evaluate its environmental and reliability claims, the expansion remains a proposal rather than new pipeline capacity. the review, and the debate over who should bear its costs and risks, now moves forward on two tracks. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.excerpt: A new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from January through June, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements.
ma-public-benefit-fraud-auditor-report-2.text: massachusetts auditor identifies $10.6m in public-benefit fraud, reports limited recoveries a new state report says investigators identified fraudulent overpayments in 402 cases from january through june, while agencies had finalized $285,339 in civil recoveries and restitution settlements. massachusetts state auditor diana dizoglio's office said wednesday that its bureau of special investigations identified $10.6 million in public-benefit fraud during the first six months of 2026, a finding that puts new numbers around losses in programs used for health care, food assistance and family support. the report covers january 1 through june 30 and is based on investigations completed by the bureau, not on criminal convictions in every case. (https://www.mass.gov/news/auditor-dizoglios-bureau-of-special-investigations-identifies-over-106-million-in-public-benefit-fraud) the bureau investigated 2,223 cases during the period and calculated overpayments in 402 cases where it identified fraud, according to the state auditor's report. masshealth and medicaid accounted for the largest share: $6,051,185, or 57% of the total. the supplemental nutrition assistance program accounted for another $3,854,119, or 36.3%. personal care attendant services represented $538,332, followed by $130,483 in transitional aid to families with dependent children and $38,463 in emergency aid to the elderly, disabled, and children. the categories add up to $10,612,582. the distribution matters because the reported losses touch programs with different administrators and different kinds of eligibility records. masshealth helps pay for medical care, snap helps eligible households buy food, and cash-assistance programs support families or people facing emergencies. a finding of an improper payment does not by itself establish who caused it or whether a criminal case will follow; the report describes the bureau's investigative findings and overpayment calculations, while other agencies handle enforcement and collection. the pace of identified fraud was higher than in the preceding six-month reporting period. boston 25 news, reviewing the new report, said the auditor's office had identified about $4.4 million in the prior period. the station also reported that the latest total included two dental providers accused of billing masshealth for “impossible days,” including days when their offices were closed. the report does not name suspected fraudsters, and the figures should be read as a snapshot of cases completed during the reporting period rather than a complete measure of all improper payments in massachusetts. (https://cmg-cmg-tv-10020-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/local/25-investigates-106m-benefits-fraud-little-clawed-back/tdd6wuwflre3xau536qiw6ac5a/) the state's recovery figures are much smaller than the amount identified. the report lists $285,339 in restitution settlements and civil recoveries for the two quarters combined, roughly 2.7% of the $10.6 million identified. that comparison does not mean the remaining amount is permanently unrecoverable: the auditor says restitution settlements continue beyond the report, and the programs that administer the benefits are responsible for collection activity. the lag does show why an investigation announcement and a completed recovery are different stages of public accountability. the quarterly split also shows where the total accumulated. in the third quarter of the state's fiscal year, the bureau investigated 994 cases and identified fraud in 168 cases, with overpayments totaling $2,981,696. in the fourth quarter, it investigated 1,229 cases and identified fraud in 234 cases, with overpayments totaling $7,630,886. the report says the fourth-quarter figures include the resumption of referrals through the document benefit fraud task force and two dental-provider cases involving alleged billing for impossible days. the bureau of special investigations operates within the office of the state auditor and can investigate allegations involving programs administered by the department of transitional assistance, the department of children and families and the division of medical assistance, which runs masshealth. its authority does not include collecting settlements or prosecuting cases. those decisions move to the relevant benefit programs and, when appropriate, state or federal prosecutors. boston 25 reported that the executive office of health and human services defended its program-integrity processes while saying agencies had referred most of the cases to the auditor's office. for residents, the report's immediate significance is less about a single statewide bill than about how quickly suspected overpayments are detected, referred and recovered. the auditor's office is asking people with information about possible public-assistance fraud to use its anonymous reporting channels, including the bureau of special investigations hotline at (617) 727-6771. the next measurable steps will be agency decisions on disqualification, civil recoupment or prosecution, along with any future reports showing how much of the identified money is ultimately recovered. massachusetts ma-salem-state-south-campus-housing-2026.excerpt: The former South Campus project will add rental housing in two phases while directing sale proceeds toward Salem State’s North Campus modernization.
ma-salem-state-south-campus-housing-2026.text: salem state redevelopment breaks ground on 473 rental homes the former south campus project will add rental housing in two phases while directing sale proceeds toward salem state’s north campus modernization. a redevelopment of salem state university’s former south campus officially moved toward construction friday, with plans for 473 new rental homes on about 23 acres along harrison road and loring avenue. the [massachusetts division of capital asset management and maintenance announced the groundbreaking](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-celebrates-groundbreaking-for-nearly-500-new-homes-on-salem-state-south-campus), and [salem patch independently reported the event](https://new.patch.com/massachusetts/salem/salem-state-south-campus-breaks-ground-473-new-rental-homes). the project is divided into two phases. avalon salem, the first phase, is planned to create 340 rental homes, with construction expected to begin this winter. the state release describes the affordability mix using 80% and 60% of area median income thresholds. those designations are affordability rules, not a promise that every unit will carry the same rent or serve the same household size. the second phase, forest river residences, is expected to add at least 133 homes. the state says at least 40% of those units will be affordable to households at or below 60% of area median income, and that phase is expected to close in 2028. that timetable describes the planned financing milestone; it is not a guaranteed occupancy date for the homes. the land is being redeveloped through the healey-driscoll administration’s state land for homes initiative, which uses surplus or underused public property for housing. the administration says the initiative had advanced plans for more than 5,600 homes during its first year. that is a pipeline figure, meaning homes in different stages of planning and development rather than units already completed or occupied. for salem, the project links a housing decision with a campus-consolidation plan. proceeds from the sale of the south campus property are expected to support capital investments on salem state’s north campus through ssu bold, the university’s long-term effort to address infrastructure needs and consolidate the campus footprint. university president john keenan said the sale allows the public institution to reinvest in teaching and learning facilities while the city gains new housing. the redevelopment has been moving through a chapter 40r smart growth overlay district. [historic salem inc.](https://historicsalem.org/advocacy/forest-river-residences/) describes the site as an active project and says the overlay sets design standards and a 20% affordability requirement for the district. the preservation group also says it is watching how the plan handles the former st. chretienne school and convent buildings and the surrounding neighborhood. those are planning and preservation concerns that will continue alongside construction; they do not change the housing totals announced for the two phases. the state’s project description says the south campus redevelopment is intended to make productive use of land no longer needed for its original institutional purpose. its local impact will depend on several later steps: the first phase must begin and complete construction, the affordability commitments must be implemented, and the second phase must reach its expected 2028 closing. the university must also translate the property proceeds into the north campus work described in its modernization plan. for now, the groundbreaking establishes a concrete schedule for a large north shore housing project. the next near-term marker is the start of avalon salem construction this winter. later updates will show when applications open, how the income-restricted units are structured, and whether forest river residences advances on the financing timeline set out by the state and developer partners. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma salem salem, massachusetts massachusetts salem housing affordable housing salem state university state land for homes campus redevelopment

ma-snap-admin-cost-shift-2026-10-01.excerpt: A federal law cuts Washington's share of state SNAP operating costs from 50% to 25%, adding an estimated $53 million to Massachusetts' current-year burden as eligibility work and call-center demand remain under pressure.
ma-snap-admin-cost-shift-2026-10-01.text: massachusetts takes on larger snap administration bill as federal share drops a federal law cuts washington's share of state snap operating costs from 50% to 25%, adding an estimated $53 million to massachusetts' current-year burden as eligibility work and call-center demand remain under pressure. massachusetts is beginning a new federal fiscal year with a larger bill for running the supplemental nutrition assistance program, after a federal law reduced washington's share of state administrative costs from 50% to 25%. the change affects the machinery behind snap — including eligibility processing, benefit issuance and related systems — rather than directly removing the federal dollars loaded onto households' electronic benefit cards. wbur reported that the shift requires massachusetts to absorb an estimated additional $53 million during the current fiscal year. the change comes from section 10106 of public law 119-21, the reconciliation law enacted in july 2025. the u.s. government publishing office's text says the federal government will cover 50% of eligible state administrative costs through fiscal year 2026, then 25% beginning in fiscal year 2027. because the federal fiscal year began oct. 1, 2026, the lower reimbursement rate is now in effect. the law is available at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/plaw-119publ21/html/plaw-119publ21.htm. the u.s. department of agriculture's food and nutrition administration described the same change in a june proposed rule. the agency said the rule would update snap regulations to match the law, while leaving the categories of allowable administrative expenses and the basic reimbursement procedures in place. the proposal is at https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/fr-062426. that distinction matters: the statute has changed the funding split, while usda's rulemaking is the regulatory step explaining how the change fits into existing program rules. for massachusetts, the new expense arrives while the agency that administers snap is already under strain. wbur reported that federal data showed enrollment in the state had fallen by nearly 190,000 after the 2025 law added eligibility requirements. the report also said the department of transitional assistance faces a lawsuit alleging that roughly 80% of snap-related calls have been dropped. those are reported conditions and allegations, not a finding that every missed call or enrollment change was caused by the cost-sharing provision. the operating-cost change is separate from the annual adjustment to household benefits. massachusetts' department of transitional assistance says the maximum monthly allotment for one person rose from $291 to $292 effective oct. 1, while the maximum for a four-person household rose from $973 to $975. the agency cautions that most households do not receive the maximum; income, shelter, utility, child-care and certain medical deductions affect the individual calculation. its table is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/snap-cost-of-living-adjustments-cola. that separation helps explain why families may see a small benefit increase even as the state faces higher administrative costs. the federal government continues to finance the underlying snap allotments, but massachusetts must find more state money for the workers, technology and customer service needed to determine eligibility and deliver those benefits. food-assistance organizations told wbur the cost shift adds pressure at a time when the department is understaffed. the law also sets up a possible second financial exposure. starting in a later fiscal year, states can be required to share part of the cost of snap benefits based on payment-error rates. wbur cited a center on budget and policy priorities estimate that massachusetts could face as much as $350 million in additional costs under that provision, but that figure is an outside estimate rather than a current bill or a final federal assessment. the timing and amount would depend on the rules and the state's measured error rate. the immediate question for massachusetts is how the administration and legislature will cover the $53 million administrative gap without slowing applications, renewals or case assistance. people receiving snap can check their current balance and notices through dta connect or the phone number on the back of their ebt card, while advocates and food banks are watching whether the added state obligation shows up as longer waits or more demand for emergency groceries. the federal cost shift is settled; its effect on service quality will become clearer as the state operates under the new funding formula. massachusetts massachusetts ma-somerville-teele-square-fire-2026-10-.excerpt: A five-alarm blaze damaged 32 homes and a row of ground-floor businesses Wednesday; the city and Somerville Homeless Coalition have opened an emergency fund as the cause remains under investigation.
ma-somerville-teele-square-fire-2026-10-.text: teele square fire displaces 43 somerville residents and closes six businesses a five-alarm blaze damaged 32 homes and a row of ground-floor businesses wednesday; the city and somerville homeless coalition have opened an emergency fund as the cause remains under investigation. somerville officials and the somerville homeless coalition have activated an emergency fund for 43 residents displaced by a five-alarm fire that damaged a teele square building wednesday. the city of somerville said thursday that the blaze affected 32 homes at 1137-1147 broadway, and that every resident escaped safely. city staff and the american red cross were helping residents find temporary accommodations and meet immediate needs. the fire began around 4:50 p.m. september 30 and continued for more than three hours, according to the cambridge-somerville independent (https://csindie.com/more-than-40-people-are-displaced-after-teele-square-fire-chief-says/). the three-story brick building, also described in reports as 1135 broadway, suffered heavy fire, smoke and water damage on its third floor and roof. the lower floors sustained extensive water damage, leaving all 32 units uninhabitable while the building is assessed and secured. the damage also shut down the building’s ground-floor retail space. the independent identified the affected businesses as blue moon smoke shop, teele square coin laundry, the happy crab and masala restaurants, and al-aswad dental; it reported that a liquor store at the far end of the building remained open. cbs boston (https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/somerville-teele-square-building-fire/) described six businesses as destroyed and reported that the building was a total loss. the differing descriptions reflect that the damage assessment was still developing, but both accounts point to a major interruption for a commercial corner that serves nearby residents. the response was unusually close to home for somerville firefighters. the city’s teele square station is across the street, and chief charles breen told cbs boston that firefighters returning from another call saw smoke and heard the building’s alarm. crews from neighboring departments were called in for mutual aid. the independent reported that five aerial ladders were used to open the roof and ventilate the structure, with assistance from departments in cambridge, arlington, boston, brookline, belmont, chelsea, everett, malden, medford, revere and watertown. several firefighters suffered minor injuries, according to the independent, and two cats were found and removed safely. no residents were reported killed. the cause had not been determined as of thursday, and breen said the fire remained under investigation. that leaves questions about how the blaze spread through the roof and whether any code, electrical or other building-system issues contributed unanswered for now. the immediate problem for residents is not only finding a place to stay but replacing household necessities while a building with 32 homes remains closed. somerville’s emergency displacement fund provides direct financial assistance to residents displaced by fires and other emergencies. the city said thursday that it is seeking financial donations through the somerville homeless coalition fund, rather than donated goods, while city workers and the red cross coordinate assistance. the fire also adds a second recovery story to a block that has carried the effects of an earlier blaze for years. the independent reported that a vacant lot known locally as “the pit,” across from the damaged building, has remained empty since a 2011 fire. a hotel proposal for that site was before the city’s zoning board of appeals on the same day as wednesday’s fire, according to the paper. that overlap does not establish a connection between the projects or the fires, but it underscores how a single emergency can affect a neighborhood already waiting on redevelopment. somerville mayor jake wilson told cbs boston that the city wants to work with property owners, tenants and business owners on a faster recovery. no reconstruction schedule or final damage estimate had been announced by thursday. for now, the confirmed next steps are temporary housing and emergency aid for displaced residents, continued fire investigation, and a broader assessment of which businesses and homes can be repaired or must be rebuilt. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma somerville teele square, somerville, massachusetts somerville teele square ma-tomorrows-teachers-scholarships-2026-.excerpt: The Tomorrow’s Teachers program offers up to $25,000 a year to eligible students in approved educator-preparation programs, but recipients must complete teaching service in Massachusetts public schools.
ma-tomorrows-teachers-scholarships-2026-.text: massachusetts opens $5 million teacher scholarship round with nov. 20 deadline the tomorrow’s teachers program offers up to $25,000 a year to eligible students in approved educator-preparation programs, but recipients must complete teaching service in massachusetts public schools. massachusetts has opened a new $5 million round of tomorrow’s teachers scholarships for students preparing to become public-school educators, the healey-driscoll administration announced oct. 1. applications are open through nov. 20. eligible students enrolled in approved educator-preparation programs at the state’s public four-year colleges and universities can receive as much as $25,000, subject to available funds and individual eligibility. the announcement makes the program relevant beyond tuition alone. the state says scholarship money can be used for expenses included in a student’s cost of attendance, including fees, room and board, books and supplies, transportation, child care and personal expenses. that broader definition matters for aspiring teachers who may be balancing coursework with family obligations, commuting or the unpaid and lower-paid portions of professional preparation. the award is not a no-strings grant. the massachusetts office of student financial assistance describes tomorrow’s teachers as a repayment-through-service scholarship: one year of teaching forgives one year of scholarship support, while a recipient who does not meet the service obligation can owe the money as a loan. the state’s program rules require recipients to pursue the appropriate massachusetts teaching credential and become a teacher of record within 12 months after completing a degree or eligible post-baccalaureate coursework. the osfa program page is available at https://www.mass.edu/osfa/programs/tmwteachers.asp. for students funded throughout a traditional four-year undergraduate path, the osfa agreement describes a four-year teaching commitment in a massachusetts public-school district. undergraduate students may receive support for up to four years, or eight semesters. students in approved post-baccalaureate preparation may receive funding for up to three semesters. those limits mean the headline maximum of $25,000 is an annual ceiling, not a promise that every applicant will receive that amount or that the program will cover every educational cost. the eligibility rules also narrow the pool. applicants must generally be massachusetts residents who meet the state’s citizenship or eligible noncitizen requirements, complete the fafsa or massachusetts application for state financial aid, enroll full time in an approved program and meet satisfactory academic progress standards. the public-college list includes bridgewater state, fitchburg state, framingham state, massachusetts college of art and design, massachusetts college of liberal arts, salem state, westfield state, worcester state and the four university of massachusetts campuses in amherst, boston, dartmouth and lowell. the program’s funding sits inside a larger state effort to build an educator pipeline. a june fact sheet from the massachusetts legislature says its fiscal 2026 fair share supplemental budget provided $10 million for tomorrow’s teachers scholarships and loan-forgiveness initiatives; the fact sheet is at https://malegislature.gov/pressroom/detail?pressreleaseid=1383. the executive branch’s new announcement identifies $5 million for the scholarship round and says a separate $7,500 loan-repayment component for eligible educators will open applications in april. those figures describe related pieces of the program, not an additional $5 million available to every scholarship applicant. the practical effect will depend on who applies, how awards are sized and whether recipients stay in massachusetts classrooms long enough to satisfy their obligations. the state is presenting the program as a way to reduce the cost of entering teaching and to strengthen and diversify the educator workforce. the available records establish the funding, rules and deadline; they do not yet show how many students will receive awards in this cycle or how many will ultimately enter public-school classrooms. prospective applicants should complete the required federal or state financial-aid application, create a massaid student portal account and review the current osfa guidelines before submitting a tomorrow’s teachers application. the immediate date to watch is nov. 20. after the application period closes, award counts and the distribution of funding among eligible public colleges will provide the first measure of demand for the new round, while later employment records will show whether the scholarship’s service bargain translates into more licensed teachers in massachusetts schools. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston ma-topsfield-giant-pumpkin-record-2026-1.excerpt: Woody Lancaster of Topsfield won the 42nd All New England Giant Pumpkin Weigh-Off in his final competition, surpassing last year’s fair record by 91 pounds.
ma-topsfield-giant-pumpkin-record-2026-1.text: topsfield fair pumpkin record falls to 2,598-pound gourd woody lancaster of topsfield won the 42nd all new england giant pumpkin weigh-off in his final competition, surpassing last year’s fair record by 91 pounds. a topsfield grower ended his competitive giant-pumpkin career by setting a new record at the fair that helped make the sport a new england fall tradition. woody lancaster’s 2,598-pound pumpkin won the 42nd all new england giant pumpkin weigh-off on oct. 2, according to the [topsfield fair’s official results](https://www.topsfieldfair.org/about/press/) and independent reporting by [the boston globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/02/metro/woody-lancaster-topsfield-fair-giant-pumpkin/). the result was a 91-pound improvement over the previous topsfield fair mark. alex noel of abington, connecticut, set that record with a 2,507-pound pumpkin in 2025; lancaster’s entry moved the fair’s winning benchmark above 2,500 pounds for the second consecutive year. the globe reported that 21 pumpkins were entered and that lancaster, 80, had said this would be his final weigh-off after decades of growing. the victory carried both a local connection and a regional field. lancaster grows his pumpkins in topsfield and has served as a longtime co-chair of the fair’s signature opening-night event. the runner-up, larry and shauna masters, entered a 2,220-pound pumpkin from just over the massachusetts line in new york. joe jutras of north scituate, rhode island, placed third with a 2,197-pound entry, while john and kerry young of jericho, vermont, finished fourth at 1,876 pounds, the globe reported. the competition also highlighted a younger grower. eleven-year-old alistair lehto of fitchburg, massachusetts, placed fifth with an 1,815-pound pumpkin and received $500 as junior grower of the year. the result gives the event a local youth angle at a moment when veteran growers are aging out. the globe reported that lancaster has mentored henry swenson, a 24-year-old topsfield grower whose pumpkin weighed 1,246 pounds this year after disease hurt the crop. the scale numbers are the culmination of a season-long project, not a quick fair stunt. lancaster told the globe that his winning pumpkin was pollinated in july, gained roughly 58 pounds a day and benefited from a different fertilizer mix in his last year. the paper reported that he can spend as much as four hours a day on the hobby. those details help explain why the weigh-off is treated as a serious agricultural contest even though the winning fruit is also a crowd-pleasing spectacle. topsfield’s event has deeper roots than the current record. the fair says the all new england giant pumpkin weigh-off began in 1984, when the winner weighed 433 pounds. the new england giant pumpkin growers association later made topsfield its official weigh-off site, and the contest now requires entries to weigh at least 300 pounds. the fair’s history notes that a 2,480-pound pumpkin set the previous record in 2022, before the 2025 and 2026 jumps. the topsfield mark is not the same as the world record. [wbur’s preview of this year’s event](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/02/topsfield-fair-giant-pumpkins-record) reported that the global mark stood at 2,819 pounds after a 2025 entry in england. lancaster’s result is therefore a fair record and a new england agricultural milestone, but it does not establish a new world best. the winning pumpkin and four runners-up will remain on display through the topsfield fair’s closing day on oct. 12, according to the globe. for the fair, the record adds a headline attraction to an 11-day event that opened with the weigh-off. for lancaster, it is a final competitive chapter: a hometown grower, at the fair’s central agricultural contest, finishing with the largest pumpkin the venue has ever weighed. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma topsfield topsfield, massachusetts massachusetts topsfield fair giant pumpkins agriculture essex county fairs

ma-westfield-freight-rail-grant-2026-10-.excerpt: MassDOT says the project could add about 1,700 railcars a year, remove an estimated 5,950 truck trips from area roads and help retain 21 jobs.
ma-westfield-freight-rail-grant-2026-10-.text: westfield quarry gets $680,000 state grant to shift more stone shipments to rail massdot says the project could add about 1,700 railcars a year, remove an estimated 5,950 truck trips from area roads and help retain 21 jobs. a westfield quarry will receive $680,000 from massachusetts to rebuild and expand an industrial rail siding, a project state transportation officials say could move more stone by train and reduce truck traffic on area roads. the grant to john s. lane & son inc., a peckham industries company, was announced oct. 1 by the massachusetts department of transportation. the work is planned at the westfield quarry, where the company already has rail access but needs larger siding capacity for expanded freight operations. massdot estimates the upgraded siding could support about 1,700 additional railcars each year. the agency also estimates that the shift from trucks to rail would eliminate roughly 5,950 truck trips annually and help retain 21 jobs. those figures are projections tied to the planned project, not a record of traffic reductions or jobs already created. the state announcement does not provide a construction start date, a completion date or a final total project cost. the announcement matters locally because quarry products are heavy and move through the region’s existing road and rail network. each train shipment can replace multiple truck movements, although the exact number depends on the material, the railcar and the delivery route. massdot says the project is expected to improve freight efficiency, reduce roadway congestion and emissions, and support continued employment at the quarry. it describes the benefit as a transportation and economic-development investment, not simply a grant to expand a private facility. the money comes through the industrial rail access program, a competitive state-funded public-private partnership administered by massdot. the program is intended for companies investing in rail infrastructure that increases use of the freight network, improves distribution efficiency and helps retain or grow industrial activity. its rules require recipients to provide matching funds equal to at least 20% of eligible project costs. the [program overview](https://www.mass.gov/industrial-rail-access-program) says applications are reviewed quarterly on a rolling basis. westfield’s freight connections give the grant a broader regional context. the pioneer valley railroad is a short-line carrier serving the westfield area, and [the westfield news reported in 2019](https://thewestfieldnews.com/pioneer-valley-railroad-gives-unique-experience/) that it handled stone, lumber, steel and other products between westfield and holyoke. that article described the railroad as moving thousands of cars annually and explained that a railcar can carry the equivalent of several truckloads. the older account provides background on the local network; it does not measure the future westfield quarry project or establish how the new siding will be operated. massdot identified the quarry as a john s. lane & son operation and says the project will rebuild and expand an existing siding. the announcement does not describe changes to public road design, truck bans or a new rail line through residential neighborhoods. it also does not specify the construction schedule or say how the private match will be financed. the next step is project implementation: rebuilding and expanding the existing siding, securing the required private match and coordinating the work with the freight railroad and quarry operations. the public announcement leaves open how long construction will take and when the added rail capacity will begin carrying shipments. for westfield and surrounding communities, the measurable test will be whether the project reaches the projected railcar volume, reduces truck movements as estimated and maintains the jobs the grant is intended to support. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma westfield westfield, massachusetts massachusetts westfield freight rail massdot quarries transportation infrastructure maine-aclu-birthright-citizenship-lawsui.excerpt: ACLU affiliates in Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts joined a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump's August order, while an earlier injunction remains in place.
maine-aclu-birthright-citizenship-lawsui.text: new england groups file fresh challenge to birthright citizenship order aclu affiliates in maine, new hampshire and massachusetts joined a federal lawsuit challenging president trump's august order, while an earlier injunction remains in place. a new federal lawsuit led in part by the aclu of maine is asking a washington, d.c., court to block the trump administration's latest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship. the case, nathan v. trump, was filed sept. 28 in the u.s. district court for the district of columbia, according to the public docket. the coalition includes the national aclu, aclu affiliates in maine, new hampshire, massachusetts and the district of columbia, the legal defense fund, the asian law caucus and the democracy defenders fund. the groups say the order violates the constitution and federal citizenship law; those are allegations in a newly filed complaint, not a ruling by the court (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2026cv03377/297026). the lawsuit targets executive order 14418, which president donald trump signed aug. 6 and the federal register published aug. 11. the order directs federal agencies not to issue documents recognizing u.s. citizenship, or accept state and local documents purporting to recognize it, when neither parent is a u.s. citizen and specified conditions apply. those conditions include a parent classified as an alien enemy, certain foreign-government or international-organization employees, and a parent alleged to have used a commercial transaction or fraud to obtain citizenship. the order also addresses some births in u.s. territories where federal law does not confer citizenship (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/eo-14418.pdf). the filing's practical reach is broader than the phrase “birth tourism” often used in public debate. the order specifically refers to arrangements in which a parent pays to ensure that a mother is in the united states to give birth or pays a surrogate who is in the country. it also gives agencies enforcement responsibilities, including the state department, justice department, department of homeland security and social security administration. if implemented, those instructions could affect how families obtain or use federal citizenship documentation, although the order's ultimate legal effect is now being contested in court. the plaintiffs' legal theory relies on the fourteenth amendment's citizenship clause and the federal statute that codifies birthright citizenship. the complaint cites the supreme court's 1898 decision in united states v. wong kim ark and says the constitution does not allow the president to create new exceptions by executive order. the filing also points to the supreme court's june decision in trump v. barbara, which the aclu says rejected the administration's earlier, broader order. the associated press separately reported that the supreme court struck down that earlier attempt before the administration issued the narrower august order (https://www.aclumaine.org/app/uploads/2026/09/nathan-v.-trump-complaint.pdf; https://apnews.com/article/trump-again-tries-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship-after-supreme-court-ruling-494add8239eb1c0c9f4ccb45db03f1f0). for new england, the case places legal organizations from three states in the next phase of the fight. aclu of maine legal director carol garvan is quoted in the group's announcement as arguing that the supreme court's decision prevents the president or congress from ending birthright citizenship. aclu affiliates are advocacy organizations, not state governments, so maine, new hampshire and massachusetts are not plaintiffs as states in this case. the regional connection is instead the participation of groups that represent or organize around immigrant-rights issues in those states (https://www.aclumaine.org/press-releases/immigrants-rights-advocates-file-federal-lawsuit-challenging-new-trump-birthright-citizenship-executive-order/). the new d.c. case follows a separate court fight over the same august order. the associated press reported that u.s. district judge deborah boardman in maryland issued a preliminary injunction on sept. 2 while a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups proceeds. maine public also reported that the maryland judge temporarily paused the order and described it as almost certainly unconstitutional. that injunction is separate from nathan v. trump; it does not mean the new case has already been decided (https://apnews.com/article/69de0a404602a6e648b35f6a852c833d; https://www.mainepublic.org/immigration/2026-09-28/aclu-of-maine-sues-trump-administration-over-latest-attempt-to-restrict-birthright-citizenship). the public d.c. docket lists the sept. 28 complaint and motions asking the court to let the plaintiffs proceed under pseudonyms and file later exhibits under seal. it did not list a merits ruling as of the docket's sept. 28 retrieval date. the next important steps will be the government's response and any decision on a request for preliminary relief. until then, the complaint records the challengers' claims, the executive order records the administration's policy, and the courts—not either side in the lawsuit—will determine whether the new restrictions can be enforced. maine maine maine me maine and new england maine new hampshire massachusetts birthright citizenship immigration federal courts aclu

me-coastal-habitat-planning-grants-2026-.excerpt: The one-time grants will fund marsh, road-crossing and natural-resource planning in Boothbay, Gouldsboro, Addison and the Popham area.
me-coastal-habitat-planning-grants-2026-.text: maine awards $299,057 for coastal habitat planning in four communities the one-time grants will fund marsh, road-crossing and natural-resource planning in boothbay, gouldsboro, addison and the popham area. maine's office of community affairs has awarded $299,057 for four coastal habitat-planning projects that officials say are intended to make communities more resilient to flooding, rising seas and infrastructure vulnerabilities. the maine coastal program's awards cover work in boothbay, gouldsboro, addison and the popham area of phippsburg, with projects scheduled to begin this fall. the [boothbay register reported the awards](https://www.boothbayregister.com/article/maine-coastal-program-announces-299057-habitat-restoration-planning-grants/274931) sept. 29, and the [maine office of community affairs describes the grant program](https://www.maine.gov/moca/funding/maine-coastal-program-habitat-restoration-planning-grant) as a one-time opportunity for planning, design and engineering. the money is not a construction award. the program's official description says eligible activities include surveys, site characterization, inventories, preliminary and final designs, project prioritization and plan preparation, while subawards do not fund construction, land acquisition or site monitoring. that distinction matters for residents: the grants can produce the engineering and information needed for future work, but they do not by themselves mean a culvert will be replaced, a marsh will be rebuilt or a road will be redesigned. in boothbay, the town will conduct a town-wide assessment of road crossings. consultants will evaluate each crossing for both coastal habitat-restoration potential and vulnerability to climate hazards, giving the town a way to rank future projects rather than treating crossings as isolated maintenance problems. the maine coastal program says its broader work includes coastwise tools for safe, cost-effective and climate-resilient tidal crossings, an issue that links transportation reliability with the health of wetlands and streams. gouldsboro's project will focus on the sand cove area and grand marsh. the plan calls for mapping sea-level-rise and storm-surge threats, basic infrastructure and natural resources, including the area's dune, freshwater and intertidal wetlands. those layers are meant to help the town understand how future coastal me-forestry-bmp-water-quality-2026-10-01.excerpt: A biennial review of 165 timber-harvesting sites found most operations using recommended safeguards, while sediment and spill risks remain concentrated in specific practices.
me-forestry-bmp-water-quality-2026-10-01.text: maine forestry report finds water-quality practices working, with gaps at stream crossings a biennial review of 165 timber-harvesting sites found most operations using recommended safeguards, while sediment and spill risks remain concentrated in specific practices. a new maine forest service report says recommended practices are generally protecting streams, lakes and wetlands during timber harvesting, but it also points to stream crossings as the place where mistakes can do the most damage. the [maine forestry best management practices use and effectiveness—data summary 2024-2025](https://digitalmaine.com/for_docs/335/) reviews field observations from 165 harvesting sites over two seasons. the [maine business gazette’s account](https://www.mainebusinessgazette.com/article/947008826-maine-forest-service-report-highlights-effectiveness-of-forestry-practices-that-protect-water-quality) reported the findings oct. 1, when the maine department of agriculture, conservation and forestry released the report. the report examines voluntary best management practices, or bmps, used for work such as stream crossings, forest roads, erosion control and sediment management. the goal is practical: keep soil, fuel and other pollutants from moving into water bodies while allowing an industry that operates across much of the state to move timber. the monitoring is not a census of every harvest. maine forest service staff select sites from harvest notifications and conduct the review during snow-free portions of the year; the agency has used the statewide program since 2000 and publishes a summary every two years. the latest sample found that 74% of sites applied appropriate practices at stream crossings. the agency emphasizes avoiding a crossing when possible because crossings carry the highest sedimentation risk. soil-movement monitoring found no sediment entering a water body in 85% of cases. sediment was recorded in the other 15%; 9% of all cases involved measurable amounts—about one cubic foot or more—and 6% involved trace amounts. those figures describe observed conditions in the sample, not a statewide estimate of every logging operation. chemical-spill results were also mostly favorable but not uniformly so. the report found no evidence of a spill at 87% of sites, a 10-percentage-point decline from the previous report. the reported events ranged from minor drips to spills covering less than 10 square feet. that change is a reminder that water-quality protection depends on more than road design: equipment handling, site supervision and quick response can affect nearby streams even when a harvest plan is otherwise sound. the comparison with the prior report is more mixed on fish passage and crossing structures. adequate structures spanning stream channels on haul roads declined 5%, while adequate crossings on operation trails increased 17%. the report also found a slight increase in sedimentation at crossing structures compared with the 2022-2023 review. when sedimentation occurred, the forest service said it most often traced the problem to inadequate bmp application during a crossing’s installation or closeout. that finding gives the report a direct operational lesson for landowners, foresters and loggers: the vulnerable moment may be the construction and removal of a crossing, not only the period when trucks are using it. the agency says it has held five statewide bmp trainings during 2024 and 2025 and plans a 2026 training focused on extreme-weather events. the planned instruction will cover structure sizing, installation and closeout, issues that become more important as intense rain can overwhelm undersized or poorly stabilized crossings. maine’s forest economy and its water resources meet at these relatively small pieces of infrastructure. a properly planned crossing can keep a harvest road usable while limiting sediment movement; a poorly installed one can connect disturbed soil directly to a stream. the new report therefore offers two conclusions at once: the state’s long-running training and monitoring program is associated with strong results in much of the sample, and continued attention is needed where the remaining failures cluster. the next step is not a new statewide rule announced in the report, but more monitoring, education and better application of existing practices. maine environment environment me maine maine forestry water quality timber harvesting stream crossings

me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.excerpt: The governor says current LIHEAP funding does not reflect sharply higher fuel costs, while Maine's latest survey puts heating oil at $5.96 a gallon after a record $6.02.
me-home-heating-costs-neada-2026-10-01.text: mills asks congress for more maine heating aid as oil prices stay near records the governor says current liheap funding does not reflect sharply higher fuel costs, while maine's latest survey puts heating oil at $5.96 a gallon after a record $6.02. maine's heating-cost story took a new turn friday when gov. janet mills asked congress to provide supplemental funding for the low-income home energy assistance program. in a letter to u.s. sens. susan collins and angus king and reps. chellie pingree and jared golden, mills said the federal money set aside for the winter does not reflect the higher fuel prices now facing maine and other cold-weather states. her request is a call for congress to act, not an approved increase in benefits. the governor's announcement is at https://www.maine.gov/governor/mills/news/governor-mills-calls-congress-boost-liheap-funding-2026-10-02. the request follows a record heating-oil price in maine. the maine department of energy resources says its statewide cash-price survey was $5.96 per gallon on september 28, after reaching a record $6.02 the previous week. the latest average is down slightly from the peak but remains far above the $3.33 average reported for the same time last year, according to bangor daily news' account of the state data. doer's survey covers delivered-fuel retailers and warns that local prices can be higher or lower; it is not a guaranteed price for every customer. the current table is at https://www.maine.gov/energy/heating-fuel-prices. the difference is consequential for a household that needs a full 275-gallon tank. mills' office says the record price adds about $740 to that fill compared with a year earlier. bangor daily news reported that this week's $5.96 average is nearly 80% above last year's level, with prices ranging from $5 to $6.30 in the state's latest regional breakdown. those figures describe spot cash prices, so pre-buy contracts, discounts, delivery fees and a home's actual consumption can produce a different bill. the new federal request builds on an earlier projection rather than replacing it. wmtw news 8, citing the national energy assistance directors association, reported september 29 that average maine heating-oil spending could reach $2,939 during the 2026-27 heating season, 77% above the $1,664 comparison figure for last winter. that is a regional estimate, not a promise that every oil-heated home will spend the same amount. weather, insulation, thermostat settings, building size, equipment efficiency and the price charged by a local supplier will all affect an individual household's costs. homes heated with propane, wood, electricity or natural gas face different price patterns. mills' letter describes the risk as especially acute in maine because roughly half of the state's homes rely on heating oil as their primary fuel and many rural homes are older. a larger fuel bill can compete with food, rent, transportation and medical expenses, while a household with little fuel left may have limited ability to wait for a better price. the governor said congress should make more liheap money available quickly; the letter does not identify a specific supplemental dollar amount or guarantee that lawmakers will approve one. maine has also begun other forms of assistance. the mills administration said october 1 that eligible low-income households will be automatically enrolled in a $40 million expansion of electric-bill discounts through supportlink and the low income assistance program. the governor's office says discounts for central maine power customers can range from 25% to 81% and for versant customers from 17% to 83%, depending on income; households served by smaller consumer-owned utilities receive the benefit differently. the announcement is at https://www.maine.gov/governor/mills/news/governor-mills-announces-automatic-electric-bill-discounts-thousands-maine-families-2026-10-01. for direct heating help, mainehousing says eligible homeowners and renters can apply for the 2026-27 home energy assistance program, supported by federal liheap funds. applications opened in august and remain available until funds are exhausted. mainehousing says crisis assistance for households with extremely low fuel supplies opens november 1 and requires a heap application first through a local community action agency. program details and income rules are at https://www.mainehousing.org/programs-services/energy/energydetails/liheap. the immediate practical question for a maine household is therefore not whether the $2,939 projection will come true, but whether help is available before a tank runs low. the governor is asking congress to increase the federal pool; the state is directing eligible residents toward heap, electric-bill discounts and its updated 2026-27 winter heating guide. until congress responds, households can compare the current local delivered-fuel price with the state's weekly benchmark and apply early, because both eligibility and available funds shape what assistance a household ultimately receives. maine maine maine me augusta maine maine heating oil home heating energy costs mainehousing heap affordability

me-maine-roads-to-quality-contract-2026-.excerpt: DHHS conditionally selected New York-based Shine Early Learning for two contracts worth an estimated $10 million, a decision that could end the University of Southern Maine's decades-long role supporting child-care providers.
me-maine-roads-to-quality-contract-2026-.text: maine child-development contracts put long-running usm program at risk dhhs conditionally selected new york-based shine early learning for two contracts worth an estimated $10 million, a decision that could end the university of southern maine's decades-long role supporting child-care providers. maine has conditionally selected an out-of-state company to take over two child-development support contracts, putting the future of maine roads to quality at the university of southern maine in doubt and raising questions about how the state will deliver training and technical help to early-childhood providers. the department of health and human services offered the contracts to shine early learning, a new york-based company whose work includes services for child-care centers, home-based providers and public schools in more than 30 states. the two awards are estimated at about $10 million over two years, according to [centralmaine.com and the portland press herald](https://www.centralmaine.com/2026/10/01/maine-dhhs-awards-child-development-grant-to-out-of-state-private-equity-backed-firm/). dhhs spokesperson lindsay hammes told the newspapers that the awards remain conditional and that the final value will be public after the contracts are completed; no contracts had been ratified when the report was published. one contract covers coaching, credentialing and training for early-childhood educators and care providers. the other would provide a dhhs-approved training plan intended to improve the quality of child-care services and the educators who provide them. those functions have been housed under one contract for much of the program's history, according to samantha warren, a university of maine system spokesperson quoted by centralmaine.com. maine roads to quality was created in 1999 through the catherine cutler institute at usm. the program provides professional development and assistance to more than 10,000 maine child-care providers each year, the newspaper reported. a [university of maine program description](https://ccids.umaine.edu/research-projects/mrtq-pdn/) says the broader professional-development network also supports a child-care database, specialized training, inclusion consultation and a warm line for providers seeking advice. the university page identifies the network's funding as a maine dhhs office of child and family services block grant. that infrastructure is tied to how maine evaluates and supports child-care quality. the [maine dhhs description of rising stars for me](https://www11.maine.gov/dhhs/ocfs/support-for-families/child-care/qris) says the quality-rating system is funded by the federal child care and development fund and administered by the department's office of child and family services. the maine department of education says public-preschool staff must join the maine roads to quality registry and describes the network as providing free or low-cost training in person, online and in hybrid formats. a change in the operator therefore affects more than a single university program; it touches a statewide system that providers use for professional development and quality-rating work. the competing proposals received sharply different scores. shine's bid earned 97 out of 100 for the coaching contract and a perfect score for the training-plan contract, while maine roads received about 73 points on each proposal, centralmaine.com reported. the state said the scores followed the process in its requests for proposals but did not explain the difference in detail. the newspaper also reported that shine's proposals were about $2 million lower across the two contracts, though dhhs has not published the final contract values because the awards are not complete. shine's applications propose using artificial intelligence in several parts of the work, including a family-navigation assistant, an employee-vetting tool and an agent to manage a provider registry, according to the report. those are plans in the company's applications, not evidence that the tools have been deployed in maine or that they will replace particular services. the contracts also require shine to employ at least 10 people in maine, a staffing condition that leaves open how much of the current locally based support model would continue. maine roads employs more than 30 people, and the university of maine system said layoffs are expected if the dhhs contracts are not renewed. the system told centralmaine.com that it plans to continue providing services through the end of the current contract and support employees who may be affected. it also plans to appeal the decision. for providers, the immediate issue is continuity: the state has announced a conditional selection, but it has not yet published a completed agreement or a transition schedule that explains when shine would assume the work. the next checkpoint is the contract process itself. dhhs will have to finalize the awards, disclose the completed values and set the terms for staffing, training, data systems and provider support. until that happens, the selection signals a possible change in who administers a core piece of maine's early-childhood infrastructure, but it does not by itself close maine roads to quality or establish exactly how services will look under the proposed new operator. maine maine maine me portland maine maine child care early childhood education maine dhhs university of southern maine state contracts artificial intelligence

me-menhaden-season-closes-quota-2026-10-.text: maine menhaden fishery set to close sunday as quota nears completion the state says harvesters have landed 98.7% of maine's available menhaden quota, extending a season shaped by a 20% coastwide cut and transfers from other states. maine's commercial atlantic menhaden season is scheduled to close sunday night after state regulators said harvesters had landed 98.7% of the available quota, a deadline that will affect the bait supply used by lobster and other coastal fisheries. the maine department of marine resources said in a september 28 notice that it expected the remaining quota to be taken after additional fishing on september 28 and october 1. the department set the closure for 11:59 p.m. sunday, october 4, and told harvesters to complete their final reports. the notice applies to all menhaden harvesters, even though the department's general 2026 season framework had listed may 1 through november 30 as the season window. the current closure notice is at https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/medmr/bulletins/42cdf35. the compressed ending reflects a difficult quota year. the atlantic states marine fisheries commission reduced the coastwide total allowable catch for 2026 to 186,840 metric tons, a 20% decrease from the prior level. maine's department of marine resources said the reduction was intended to lower fishing mortality while protecting predators such as striped bass. maine's preliminary state quota was set at 19,599,137 pounds, with another 4,119,117 pounds reserved for its episodic event set-aside program. the agency's management page is https://www.maine.gov/dmr/fisheries/commercial/fisheries-by-species/menhaden-atlantic/menhaden-management. maine officials also said transfers from partner states helped keep the directed fishery open into october. the department said it received twice as much transferred quota as in the previous effort, despite the coastwide reduction. that choice allowed fishermen to keep using purse seines rather than shifting in mid-september to the small-scale provision, which carries different gear and quota rules. the state described the decision as a way to preserve additional harvest opportunity while staying within the available allocation. the stakes extend beyond the boats that catch menhaden. the atlantic states marine fisheries commission describes menhaden as a forage species for striped bass, bluefish and weakfish, and says commercial bait landings are used mostly in lobster, crab and hook-and-line fisheries. the commission's species overview says the 2026 quota has a zero-percent modeled chance of overfishing under its current assessment, while the stock is not classified as overfished. those findings do not remove the economic effect of a smaller quota on bait users. seafoodsource reported that maine lobster groups viewed the 20% cut as less severe than proposals for reductions of more than 50%, while still warning that any cut could affect the small-boat fleet: https://www.seafoodsource.com/news/supply-trade/asmfc-cuts-atlantic-menhaden-quota-by-20-percent-in-2026. the next debate is already underway. the commission has scheduled a virtual public hearing for 6 p.m. thursday, october 1, on draft addendum ii to the interstate menhaden plan. the proposal considers reducing the chesapeake bay reduction-fishery cap by as much as 50% and distributing that cap more evenly over the fishing season. the commission says the options are intended to address concentrated fishing effort and possible ecological effects in the bay. public comments are due by 11:59 p.m. october 9. hearing and comment details are available at https://asmfc.org/events/general-public-hearing-on-atlantic-menhaden-draft-addendum-ii/. for maine harvesters, the immediate question is operational: how much quota remains after the final scheduled fishing day and how will the closure affect bait inventories heading into the fall lobster season. the department of marine resources has not announced an extension beyond october 4 in its current notice. longer-term decisions will come through the interstate process, with the commission expected to discuss menhaden quotas for 2027 and 2028 during its october 2026 annual meeting. maine maine maine me maine coastal fisheries maine atlantic menhaden commercial fishing lobster fishery fishing me-paid-family-medical-leave-first-claim.text: maine paid-leave program logs 8,376 applications in first report the new statewide benefit approved 4,720 claims during its first three months of data, while officials said the trust fund is projected to remain stable for the next decade. maine's new paid family and medical leave program received 8,376 applications during its first three months of claims activity, giving workers and employers the first detailed look at how the benefit is being used. the maine department of labor published the figures oct. 1 in the program's first claims administration report, alongside a new actuarial report that projects the program's trust fund will remain stable for the next 10 years. the claims period ran from march 30 through june 30, 2026, according to the department's [announcement](https://www.maine.gov/labor/news%5fevents/article.shtml?id=13363661). the early numbers are a launch snapshot, not a full-year measure. workers could begin submitting applications march 30, but benefits became payable only for leave taken on or after may 1. of the 8,376 submissions, 511 were later canceled and 682 were filed with the public administrator by workers covered by an approved private plan. another 691 were still awaiting a decision when the data was pulled, leaving 6,492 decided claims. the report says the next annual report, due oct. 1, 2027, will cover a full year from july 1, 2026, through june 30, 2027. among the decided claims, 4,720, or 72.7%, were approved and 1,772, or 27.3%, were denied. the most common denial reason was missing documentation: 57.5% of denied claims fell into that category. other denials involved earnings requirements, exhausted leave, identity verification, documentation that did not establish eligibility, or timing rules. the report says 6.7% of denials involved an identity that could not be verified, while some applications sought payment for leave before the may 1 benefit date. those figures describe the first administrative experience and may change as workers, employers and the claims administrator become more familiar with the system. medical leave was the largest approved category. the report attributes 42.4% of approved claims to medical conditions other than pregnancy, 14.9% to pregnancy, 30.7% to bonding with a child through birth, adoption or foster care, and 11.6% to caring for a family member with a serious health condition. safe leave accounted for 0.4% and military family leave for 0.1%. the average weekly benefit across approved claims was $816.33. continuous leave made up 86.49% of approved claims, compared with 11.88% for intermittent leave and 1.63% for reduced schedules. these categories come from the [claims report](https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/docs/2026/claimsadministrationannualreport2026.pdf). the report also offers an early, limited demographic picture. workers ages 26 to 41 submitted 54.3% of claims, the largest age group, followed by workers ages 42 to 57 at 23.4%. women submitted 62.9% of claims, men 33.9%, and 0.4% came from applicants identifying as nonbinary; 2.8% did not provide a gender response. race data was less complete: 58.8% of applicants declined to answer, while 38.6% selected white. the department cautions that the small initial data set can overrepresent particular circumstances and that future reports may shift those proportions. maine's program was created by a 2023 law and provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for their own serious health condition, pregnancy, bonding with a new child, caring for a family member, qualifying military-family needs or safety-related leave. the department of labor administers the program, with aflac handling claims administration, according to the report. the earlier [actuarial report](https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/docs/2025/mepfmlactuaryreport.pdf) describes the funding structure: employers with at least 15 workers contribute 1% of wages and may deduct up to half from employees, while smaller employers contribute 0.5% and may deduct that full amount. the new actuarial projection is intended to answer the program's central financial question as benefits begin: whether contributions and investment income can keep pace with claims and administration. its baseline table projects a net fund balance of $304.5 million at the end of 2026, rising to $448.1 million at the end of 2036. those are projections, not cash already held or a guarantee of future rates; they depend on assumptions about payroll, claims, benefits and expenses. the department of labor characterized the trust fund as solvent and stable for the next decade, while the claims report says the coming full-year data will provide a more useful test of early assumptions. for maine workers, the immediate practical takeaway is that the benefit is operating but documentation and plan eligibility matter. the department says workers, employers and self-employed people can get help through the program website and separate benefits and contributions portals. as more claims mature, the state will have to show whether processing times, approval patterns and the fund's projected cushion hold across a full year rather than a three-month launch period. independent coverage by [the maine wire](https://www.themainewire.com/2026/10/nearly-5000-mainers-took-paid-family-leave-from-april-through-june/) likewise reported the first approval totals and benefit mix, while noting that the initial report is too short to settle longer-term questions about cost and use. new-england new-england new england me augusta maine maine paid leave family leave medical leave workers labor policy

me-state-archives-open-access-2026-10-01.text: maine state archives launches online portal for more than 100,000 public records the new open access platform brings digitized and born-digital state records into one searchable site, while the archives continue a much larger preservation effort. maine’s state archives has launched a public online portal that puts more than 100,000 imaged government and historical records in one searchable place. secretary of state shenna bellows announced the official launch of open access on oct. 1, describing it as the public-facing part of a broader effort to preserve and provide long-term access to records held by the state. statescoop independently reported the rollout as an expansion of online access to maine records. the platform is available at [digitalarchives.maine.gov](https://digitalarchives.maine.gov/). visitors can search the collection, browse by category and use list, timeline, gallery or map views. the site groups materials into areas including the executive and legislative branches, courts, land and natural resources, social history, military records, elections, statehood and government administration. the [maine state archives’ digital-records page](https://www.maine.gov/sos/archives/digital-archives) says documents in the online collection are public records and free to download. the launch is significant because it covers both digitized material and records that were created electronically in the first place. that distinction matters for a government archive: scanning older paper documents makes them easier to use, while preserving born-digital files helps prevent newer public records from becoming inaccessible as software and storage systems change. maine officials describe open access as part of a strategic digital-preservation system for records that are archival or subject to long-term retention. the historical range is unusually broad. the secretary of state’s announcement points to collections stretching from a 1639 royal land grant to the 2024 papers of the lewiston tragedy commission. other examples include revolutionary war land grants, records from maine’s civil war history and documents tied to the state’s development. those materials can serve different audiences: genealogists tracing families, students working with primary sources, researchers studying public policy and residents seeking a record of how state institutions operated. the new portal does not mean the entire archive is online. the maine state archives says it cares for approximately eight miles of official state records, and officials acknowledge that much remains to be digitized. the launch announcement says open access currently contains just over 100,000 imaged records and will grow as more collections are scanned. the archives’ broader digital-archives information page separately reported more than one million individual records in its online collection as of march 1, a larger figure that includes the state’s wider digital-access work rather than only the newly highlighted imaged records on open access. that difference gives readers a useful way to understand the project’s scale: open access is a new front door, not a finished inventory. its search tools can make records discoverable without a trip to augusta, but the results will still depend on what has been processed, described and digitized. the [archives’ research guidance](https://www.maine.gov/sos/archives/archives-services) says the facility is a closed-stacks, non-circulating archive and that researchers should make appointments so staff can retrieve materials; the online catalog’s coverage will change as new collections are added. for maine communities, the practical benefit is a shorter path between a question and the original record. a resident investigating a land transaction, a teacher building a lesson about statehood or a researcher checking an agency decision can begin with the same public platform. the next phase is continued digitization and preservation: expanding the searchable holdings while keeping the records authentic, usable and available for future generations.
