me-winter-warming-shelter-awards-2026-09.excerpt: The MaineHousing grants will support 12 organizations in eight homeless-service hubs, but Bangor reporting shows that some local warming centers still face funding and capacity gaps.
me-winter-warming-shelter-awards-2026-09.text: maine awards record $2.72m for winter warming shelters and 474 beds the mainehousing grants will support 12 organizations in eight homeless-service hubs, but bangor reporting shows that some local warming centers still face funding and capacity gaps. mainehousing has awarded $2,722,538 to 12 organizations that will provide 474 beds at short-term warming shelters this winter, the largest funding total and bed count since the state program began five years ago. the [maine state housing authority's announcement](https://www.mainehousing.org/news/news-detail/2026/09/30/mainehousing-awards--2.72-million-for-winter-warming-shelters) says the grants reach eight of maine's nine homeless-service hubs. most of the shelters are expected to operate overnight through april 30, giving people experiencing homelessness or housing instability a place to get out of dangerous cold. the awards are operating support, not a promise that 474 beds will be open every night regardless of weather or local staffing. mainehousing says recipients may use the money for staff, supplies, transportation, longer hours and other shelter costs. grant recipients will coordinate with municipalities, emergency managers and community partners when conditions become hazardous. that arrangement matters because a warming shelter is an emergency-weather resource, not the same thing as a permanent shelter or a year-round housing placement. bangor illustrates both the reach and the limits of the new round. the [bangor daily news reported](https://www.bangordailynews.com/2026/09/29/bangor/bangor-government/bangor-warming-centers-state-funding/) that the brick church will receive $427,650 to support 65 beds, while the bangor area homeless shelter will receive $10,000 for five beds. together, the two awards total $437,650, more than any other maine city received. the mansion church and together place also applied but were not awarded state funds, leaving uncertainty about how the city's full network will operate. that uncertainty is tied to demand rather than just a budget line. bangor's homeless response coordinator told the bangor daily news that the city's four warming centers served roughly 80 to 90 people per night last year. the report said the city had to provide emergency money last year after the brick church's request was denied, helping keep that center open and allowing together place to operate an overnight center for the first time. this year's larger state award improves the outlook for some sites, but it does not automatically cover every location that people may rely on during a cold snap. local operators told [wabi](https://www.wagmtv.com/2026/10/01/bangor-warming-shelters-prepare-winter-state-awards-record-grants/) that capacity remains a practical concern. pastor leon licata of the brick church said the church can hold about 70 people, while 120 to 130 people were outside during one period last year. pastor terry dinkins of the mansion church said his center plans to open even without a state grant, though it may need community donations and other changes to keep doing so. those accounts describe local plans and reported conditions; they are not a statewide count of unmet shelter demand. mainehousing director dan brennan said dangerous winter weather can put people at risk, particularly those without stable housing. the agency's broader winter guidance also points to the home energy assistance program and energy crisis intervention program for eligible households that need help with heating costs or an emergency. those programs address a different problem from a warming shelter: of energy resources' winter-resources page](https://www1.maine.gov/energy/winter-heating-resources) says warming centers are normally opened for a specific emergency or event when temperatures, wind ne-dupont-vylor-pfas-removal-2026-10-03.excerpt: Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont joined a case alleging that a seed-business spin-off left PFAS liabilities behind; the defendants now challenge the state-court forum.
ne-dupont-vylor-pfas-removal-2026-10-03.text: dupont, corteva move pfas asset lawsuit involving five new england states to federal court maine, massachusetts, new hampshire, rhode island and vermont joined a case alleging that a seed-business spin-off left pfas liabilities behind; the defendants now challenge the state-court forum. a legal fight involving five new england states over who will bear the costs of alleged pfas contamination has shifted from indiana state court to federal court. dupont, corteva and the newly created seed company vylor removed the lawsuit after a coalition of attorneys general sued over the companies’ oct. 1 separation of the pioneer seeds business. [inside epa](https://insideepa.com/pfas-news/dupont-defendants-remove-vylor-fraudulent-transfer-case-us-court) reported the removal and the defendants’ jurisdictional arguments on oct. 2. the case is now listed as 1:26-cv-02122 in the u.s. district court for the southern district of indiana. the original complaint was filed by indiana and 14 other states, plus guam, according to the [vermont attorney general’s office](https://ago.vermont.gov/blog/2026/10/01/attorney-general-clark-joins-multistate-fraudulent-transfer-lawsuit-against-dupont-corteva-and-newly). the new england plaintiffs are maine, massachusetts, new hampshire, rhode island and vermont. they are challenging a corporate transaction, not announcing a new drinking-water advisory or a new contamination finding in those states. their complaint alleges that eidp, the legal entity historically known as dupont, and its parent corteva moved valuable assets into vylor while leaving major pfas-related liabilities with the older companies. the dispute follows corteva’s separation of its seed business into vylor. the vermont release says the transferred business represented roughly three-quarters of the value remaining in dupont and corteva, while vylor assumed none of the pfas liabilities at issue in the states’ claims. those descriptions are allegations from the plaintiffs, not findings by a court. corteva’s [oct. 1 form 8-k](https://www.sec.gov/archives/edgar/data/30554/000119312526409549/d23835d8k.htm) separately confirms that the separation was completed and records that states had sought restraints on the transfer and on later asset dispositions. the states are seeking immediate limits on what the companies can do with the assets while the case proceeds. the proposed temporary restraining order would freeze the transferred seed assets, prevent vylor from selling or pledging them, and restrict dupont and corteva from using remaining funds for dividends or stock buybacks, the vermont attorney general said. the requested relief is designed to preserve a pool of assets that the states say could be needed for cleanup, monitoring and other costs if they ultimately win their pfas claims. the defendants’ removal changes the court handling the dispute but does not decide whether the states’ claims are valid. inside epa reported that the companies cited federal-officer jurisdiction and said they intend to rely on the government-contractor defense. those are defense positions, not rulings. the federal docket’s case description identifies the matter as a fraud action, while the states’ complaint characterizes the transfer as a fraudulent conveyance intended to put assets beyond the reach of creditors. the court has not resolved those competing descriptions. the companies’ public filings provide important context for the stakes. in its sec filing, corteva says natural-resource-damage lawsuits involving eidp, chemours and related companies have been brought by attorneys general in 31 states, the district of columbia and three territories. the filing also says some cases include fraudulent-conveyance claims and seek reimbursement for monitoring and remediation, damages tied to natural resources and punitive damages. that disclosure describes pending litigation; it does not concede the states’ allegations in the new indiana case. for new england, the immediate significance is that five state governments are asking a court to protect assets before a larger pfas-liability record is resolved. pfas are a broad class of persistent chemicals used in products designed to resist heat, oil, stains and water, according to the vermont attorney general. the region has its own water-treatment and cleanup disputes, but this case is about corporate responsibility and access to assets rather than a new regional exposure warning. residents should not treat the filing as a change in tap-water guidance. the next steps will be procedural as well as substantive. the federal court must address the removal and the states’ request for temporary restraints before the parties can move deeper into the merits. a ruling on the requested order would not by itself establish pfas liability; it would determine whether assets remain restricted while the case continues. the companies can contest the states’ claims, and the plaintiffs would still have to prove their allegations. until the court acts, the separation remains completed but the fight over its legal consequences is active. new-england environment environment new england and indiana new england pfas ne-fuel-economy-lawsuit-2026-10-02.excerpt: Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Vermont are among 26 states and local governments challenging NHTSA’s weaker mileage standards for new cars and light trucks.
ne-fuel-economy-lawsuit-2026-10-02.text: new england states join lawsuit over federal fuel-economy rule connecticut, maine, massachusetts, rhode island and vermont are among 26 states and local governments challenging nhtsa’s weaker mileage standards for new cars and light trucks. five new england states have joined a federal lawsuit challenging a new national highway traffic safety administration rule that lowers the fuel-economy requirements for new passenger cars and light trucks. connecticut, maine, massachusetts, rhode island and vermont are part of a coalition of 26 states, counties and cities that filed a petition for review oct. 2 in the u.s. court of appeals for the first circuit. the [connecticut attorney general’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-challenges-trump-rollback-of-fuel-economy-standards) and [vermont attorney general’s office](https://ago.vermont.gov/blog/2026/10/02/attorney-general-clark-joins-lawsuit-challenging-trump-administrations-rollback-fuel-economy) announced their states’ participation. the case targets nhtsa’s final corporate average fuel economy, or cafe, rule. cafe is a manufacturer-level program: automakers must meet an average fuel-economy requirement across the cars and light trucks they sell, rather than making every individual vehicle achieve one identical mileage figure. the agency’s [official program summary](https://www.nhtsa.gov/laws-regulations/corporate-average-fuel-economy) says the 2026 rule projects an industry fleetwide average requirement of about 34.9 miles per gallon in model year 2031. nhtsa also says it will end inter-manufacturer credit trading beginning in model year 2028 and revise fleet classifications beginning in 2030. the states describe those changes as a weakening of long-standing requirements. in the petition, massachusetts attorney general andrea campbell and the other parties argue that nhtsa failed to follow the energy policy and conservation act’s instruction to set standards at the “maximum feasible” level. they also allege that the agency’s analysis is arbitrary and capricious and violates the federal administrative procedure act. those are allegations in a pending case, not findings by the court. the legal dispute turns partly on how the agency measured the existing vehicle fleet and the technology available to improve it. vermont attorney general charity clark’s office says the rule improperly requires nhtsa to ignore the presence of millions of electric vehicles when it evaluates what level of fuel economy is feasible. the [massachusetts petition](https://www.mass.gov/doc/nhtsa-petition/download) says the coalition is challenging the rule’s treatment of fleet performance, fuel savings, vehicle affordability and related assumptions. nhtsa’s public summary presents the rule as an effort to bring the cafe program into compliance with federal law. the regional stakes are both practical and industrial. new england drivers would encounter the rule through the fuel efficiency of vehicles sold in coming model years, while manufacturers and dealerships would make product and compliance decisions under the revised standards. the states contend that weaker requirements can increase gasoline use and leave households more exposed to oil-price swings. connecticut attorney general william tong’s office also points to the rule’s elimination of credit trading as a threat to electric-vehicle industries and other businesses that rely on a predictable national market. those economic and consumer effects remain contested claims that the litigation will test. the challenge arrives as the region is already pursuing its own transportation and climate policies. massachusetts, rhode island and vermont have adopted or pursued vehicle-emissions rules that are more protective than federal baselines, while connecticut and maine are also participating in regional clean-transportation planning. a federal cafe rule does not by itself cancel state air-pollution authorities, but it can change the nationwide floor for vehicle efficiency and complicate the market assumptions behind state programs. the lawsuit therefore reaches beyond a technical mileage formula into the states’ broader effort to reduce transportation emissions and fuel costs. the coalition is led by california and includes attorneys general from states across the country, along with chicago, denver, new york city and the city and county of san francisco. [california’s attorney general](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-bonta-files-lawsuit-challenging-trump-administration%e2%80%99s-rollback) listed the same 26-state-and-local-government coalition and said the petition was filed in the first circuit. independent coverage by [the associated press](https://apnews.com/article/936f05f9284bf4ba49806b4a6070b8da) reported a separate lawsuit by environmental groups over the same federal rule, underscoring that the administration faces more than one legal challenge. the new rule does not immediately change the mileage of cars already on new england roads, and the lawsuit does not by itself suspend the rule. the court could leave the standards in place while the case proceeds, or later order changes if the challengers prevail. the next important steps will be the federal government’s response and any request for a stay or other interim relief. until the court acts, automakers, states and consumers will be watching how the revised standards are implemented and whether the first circuit accepts the coalition’s argument that nhtsa set the bar below what federal law requires. new-england new-england new england new england and the first circuit new england fuel economy cafe standards nhtsa connecticut massachusetts maine rhode island vermont

ne-new-england-nuclear-policy-summit-202.excerpt: Energy officials from all six states met at UMass Lowell, but the region’s new nuclear conversation is still a policy exploration rather than a construction plan.
ne-new-england-nuclear-policy-summit-202.text: new england states weigh nuclear revival against cost and siting barriers energy officials from all six states met at umass lowell, but the region’s new nuclear conversation is still a policy exploration rather than a construction plan. new england’s six states are taking a closer look at advanced nuclear power as electricity demand rises, but a regional summit this week underscored how far the idea remains from a new reactor breaking ground. officials from connecticut, maine, massachusetts, new hampshire, rhode island and vermont met sept. 30 at the university of massachusetts lowell for a policy summit organized with the national governors association. the meeting brought state energy officials together with researchers, industry representatives, local-government voices and environmental organizations. umass lowell said the participants discussed future electricity needs, advanced reactor technologies, safety, community engagement, federal and international perspectives, and possible business models for adding nuclear generation to the regional grid. the university’s oct. 2 account described the gathering as a forum to examine options, not an approval for a particular facility or project site. the summit follows a march statement from the six governors that called for cooperation on keeping existing nuclear plants operating safely and affordably while exploring advanced technologies. that statement points to a basic regional tension: new england wants to cut emissions and maintain reliable power, but the transition is also beginning to push electricity demand higher. iso new england, the grid operator, has identified growing winter demand as a planning concern, while state officials told wbur that demand is rising after years in which regional electricity use had generally been flat. nuclear power already supplies a substantial share of the region’s electricity. the two remaining commercial stations are millstone in waterford, connecticut, and seabrook in new hampshire. their three reactors together produce nearly 3,300 megawatts, or about one-quarter of new england’s generation, according to ct mirror’s reporting on the summit. that existing fleet gives the region experience with nuclear operations, but it also highlights the scale of any replacement or expansion effort after a long period without a new commercial reactor in the northeast. supporters see advanced nuclear designs as one possible source of dependable, low-carbon electricity for a grid that is also adding electric vehicles, heat pumps and other loads. the concept includes small modular reactors and other designs intended to be more standardized than the large plants built in the last century. state officials have not identified a new england project that is ready for construction, and the summit did not create a procurement program, set a target for new megawatts or commit ratepayer funds. the obstacles are unusually specific to the region. ct mirror reported that massachusetts, maine, rhode island and vermont have restrictions requiring legislative or voter approval before a new nuclear reactor could be built. connecticut has loosened its rules for advanced reactors, including by allowing communities to vote on whether to explore hosting one, but no municipality has used that option. a proposal would therefore have to clear state law, federal licensing, local politics, environmental review and a long-term plan for radioactive waste. money is another barrier. new england’s deregulated electricity markets generally separate power generation from the utilities that deliver electricity, unlike the market structure under which the region’s existing reactors were built. that makes it harder to decide who would finance a new plant and how construction risk would be allocated. the recent u.s. experience also weighs on the debate: the vogtle reactors in georgia entered service in the last decade after years of delay and a total cost above $30 billion, according to federal energy data cited by ct mirror. the public response remains divided. wbur reported that protesters gathered outside the lowell summit with signs opposing nuclear power and a mock nuclear-waste cask, while the meeting itself emphasized safety and public trust. that tension matters because a regional policy agreement cannot substitute for community consent. even a technically promising reactor design would need a host community, a regulator-approved site and a financing structure that residents and customers consider credible. for households and businesses, the immediate consequence is not a new power plant but a new phase of regional planning. new england’s officials are trying to keep existing nuclear generation available while testing whether newer designs could fit a grid facing higher demand and limited options for firm, non-fossil power. that approach leaves open several questions: whether advanced reactors will become affordable, whether any community will volunteer to host one, and whether the states can agree on a regional financing model. the next steps are expected to involve continued coordination among state energy offices, iso new england, federal agencies, researchers and potential developers. the governors’ march statement calls for exploring financing, public-private partnerships and regulatory approaches, while the lowell summit’s organizers said the meeting would support further implementation work. until those discussions produce a specific project, schedule and approval path, new england’s nuclear revival remains a long-range policy option rather than a construction announcement. sources: [university of massachusetts lowell](https://www.uml.edu/news/press-releases/2026/ngasummitrelease100226.aspx), [ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/02/new-england-not-likely-to-see-nuclear-power-revival-any-time-soon/), [wbur](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/01/nuclear-power-summit-new-england-hesitation), [new england governors’ statement](https://www.mass.gov/doc/new-england-governors-nuclear-statement/download), and [iso new england nuclear overview](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/100035/2026%5f04%5f23%5fiso%5fnuclear%5f101.pdf). new-england new-england new england new england and lowell, nh-bobcat-poaching-guilty-2026-10-02.excerpt: Federal prosecutors say at least 41 bobcats were illegally killed in New Hampshire, falsely tagged in New York and shipped to Canada for sale.
nh-bobcat-poaching-guilty-2026-10-02.text: three men plead guilty in new hampshire bobcat-poaching scheme federal prosecutors say at least 41 bobcats were illegally killed in new hampshire, falsely tagged in new york and shipped to canada for sale. three new hampshire men pleaded guilty this week in a federal case that prosecutors say involved the illegal killing of at least 41 bobcats and the shipment of their pelts to canada. the pleas add a major development to a long-running wildlife investigation spanning new hampshire, new york and canada. the [u.s. attorney’s office for the district of new hampshire](https://www.justice.gov/usao-nh/pr/three-men-plead-guilty-poaching-more-40-bobcats-and-exporting-them-canada) announced the pleas friday. sherwood dubrey jr., 48, and randy inman, 49, pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the federal lacey act. sherwood dubrey sr., 72, pleaded guilty to a lacey act violation. all three appeared before u.s. district judge joseph n. laplante, and the court scheduled their sentencings for january 2027. the younger dubrey and inman each face a maximum of five years in prison and up to three years of supervised release. the elder dubrey faces a maximum of one year in prison and up to one year of supervised release. those are statutory maximums, not predictions of the sentences the judge will impose. according to the federal account, dubrey jr. and inman killed bobcats in new hampshire from 2018 through 2022, then moved the pelts to new york. dubrey sr. allegedly obtained false cites tags there so the animals would appear to have been legally taken in a state with a bobcat hunting season. the pelts were then exported to canada and offered at a fur auction. prosecutors say the scheme involved at least 41 illegally exported pelts. [new hampshire public radio](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-02/poaching-bobcats-nh-newhampshire-operation-night-cat) independently reported the same sequence and described the case as one of the state’s largest recent poaching investigations. the case matters because new hampshire does not allow bobcat hunting or trapping. the justice department says the lacey act, enacted in 1900, prohibits wildlife violations that cross state or international borders. a lawfully harvested bobcat pelt also requires a tag under the convention on international trade in endangered species, or cites. new york has a legal bobcat season and an export program, while new hampshire has neither because taking the animals is unlawful. the alleged movement of pelts across state lines therefore was not a paperwork technicality; it was central to making illegally taken wildlife appear eligible for international trade. investigators say the animals were lured with bait piles placed on the men’s property and on state land before being shot. the justice department said text messages and photographs or videos from rifles with scopes documented the conduct, and that messages showed the defendants knew the killings were illegal. new hampshire fish and game conservation officers and the u.s. fish and wildlife service led the investigation, with assistance from agencies in new york, canada and massachusetts as well as the fbi. the federal release attributes those details to the public record and investigative evidence; northeast news has not independently reviewed the underlying files. nhpr reported that the federal pleas are part of operation night cat, a new hampshire fish and game investigation that previously produced state convictions in 2024 for related hunting violations. inman and dubrey jr. are former corrections officers at the new hampshire state prison for men, according to nhpr. the public radio report also said the broader investigation uncovered allegations of potential crimes by prison staff that authorities reviewed but did not charge. those separate allegations are not part of the federal bobcat pleas and should not be treated as proven conduct. the wildlife backdrop is unusually clear in state records. new hampshire fish and wildlife’s [2023-24 furbearer report](https://www.nhfishandwildlife.com/assets/performance-reports/w89r21-projects%205-8%20combined%20final%202024.pdf) says the bobcat season remained closed; trappers reported 36 incidental captures that were released and one bobcat reported killed. that dated report is not a current population estimate, but it explains why the state treats unauthorized killing as a conservation and enforcement issue rather than an unregulated harvest. federal officials also said the case threatened the tagging system used to keep wildlife trade legal and sustainable. the next formal step is sentencing in january. the justice department says the investigation involved cooperation across multiple jurisdictions, underscoring why wildlife cases can become federal matters when animals or pelts cross borders. the guilty pleas resolve the defendants’ responsibility for the charges to which they admitted, but the judge will still determine penalties. for new hampshire, the case leaves a concrete reminder that the state’s closed bobcat season applies even when a pelt is later moved somewhere that has different hunting rules—and that false origin documents do not erase where protected wildlife was actually taken. new-hampshire environment environment nh concord new hampshire new hampshire bobcats wildlife conservation poaching lacey act nh fish and game

nh-drought-persists-after-noreaster-2026.excerpt: The latest U.S. Drought Monitor update says 96.05% of the state remains abnormally dry, with more than half in moderate drought after the weekend storm.
nh-drought-persists-after-noreaster-2026.text: new hampshire drought lingers despite nor’easter rain the latest u.s. drought monitor update says 96.05% of the state remains abnormally dry, with more than half in moderate drought after the weekend storm. a weekend nor’easter delivered at least an inch of rain to most of new hampshire, but it did little to change the state’s drought picture. as of oct. 1, 96.05% of new hampshire was at least abnormally dry and 53.33% was in moderate drought, according to the latest update summarized by [wmur](https://www.wmur.com/article/new-hampshire-drought-noreaster-report-101/73982475). the figures describe the share of the state’s land area in each category, not the percentage of residents or individual properties affected. the limited change matters because a single storm can improve surface moisture without repairing longer-term deficits in streams, reservoirs, groundwater and soils. wmur reported that the rainfall brought few gains to northern new england, while wetter conditions farther south improved portions of connecticut, massachusetts and rhode island. maine and new hampshire remained broadly dry, although maine’s conditions were more severe in the report’s regional comparison. the u.s. drought monitor classifies abnormally dry conditions as d0. d0 is not technically drought, but it can describe a landscape that is unusually dry or recovering from drought. moderate drought is d1, the first formal drought category. the monitor says d1 can bring some damage to crops and pastures, higher fire risk, low streams, reservoirs or wells, and developing or imminent water shortages in some places. those are broad indicators; they do not mean every new hampshire community or household is experiencing the same conditions. more information is available through the [u.s. drought monitor’s current map and data tools](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/). the latest statewide percentages also mask a sharp geographic contrast. wmur reported that just under 4% of new hampshire had no drought conditions, concentrated in a small area in southwestern hillsborough county and part of cheshire county. in other words, a resident may see a different situation depending on the watershed, soil, elevation and water source serving a particular town. the statewide map is useful for tracking the regional pattern, but local water managers and emergency officials are the authorities for specific restrictions or well concerns. new hampshire’s current conditions are nevertheless better than they were at this point last year. wmur reported that nearly the entire state had been in severe or extreme drought in late september 2025, with central new hampshire among the hardest-hit areas. the comparison shows why the current report should be read as a measure of ongoing stress rather than a declaration that the state is facing the same level of crisis as last fall. the u.s. drought monitor is updated weekly from a combination of precipitation, soil-moisture, streamflow, groundwater and other indicators. its maps are released on thursdays after a tuesday morning data cutoff, so the oct. 1 assessment captures conditions through the latest reporting cycle rather than every hour of rainfall. that timing also means a future wet period could change the map, while a short burst of rain may not be enough to move deeper hydrologic measures. for residents, the next developments to watch are not just the next rain total but whether water levels recover across the systems that supply farms, forests, fire departments and homes. people who rely on private wells should use their town or state notices for local guidance instead of treating a statewide percentage as a diagnosis of their own supply. the immediate message from the latest report is narrower: the nor’easter offered some rain, but it did not end new hampshire’s dry spell, and more sustained moisture will be needed for a broader recovery. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester new hampshire new hampshire drought weather water supply climate

nh-medicaid-premiums-federal-approval-20.excerpt: A premium system that was expected to start July 1 has no new launch date while the state waits for federal approval and answers about how it fits with new Medicaid cost-sharing rules.
nh-medicaid-premiums-federal-approval-20.text: new hampshire medicaid premiums remain on hold awaiting federal guidance a premium system that was expected to start july 1 has no new launch date while the state waits for federal approval and answers about how it fits with new medicaid cost-sharing rules. new hampshire’s planned medicaid premium system remains on hold because the state is still waiting for federal guidance on how the charges would interact with changes made by congress. the department of health and human services has not begun collecting the premiums and has not announced a new start date, according to an oct. 1 report by the [new hampshire bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/01/lacking-federal-approval-new-hampshire-forced-to-hold-off-on-new-medicaid-premiums/). jake leon, a dhhs spokesperson, told the bulletin that the situation is “status quo” and that the department is still waiting for guidance on the impact of h.r. 1, the federal law commonly called the one big beautiful bill act. the premiums had been expected to take effect july 1. the delay means eligible granite advantage members are not currently receiving bills under the new system, even though the state law authorizing the charges remains in place. new hampshire law directs dhhs to seek a medicaid waiver and, if necessary, a state-plan amendment to charge premiums to granite advantage participants with household income at or above 100% of the federal poverty level. the statute sets monthly amounts of $60 for a one-person household, $80 for two people, $90 for three people and $100 for a household of four or more during the biennium ending june 30, 2027. it also requires the department to develop hardship criteria. the [new hampshire general court’s text of rsa 126-aa:2-a](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/x/126-aa/126-aa-2-a.htm) makes the charges subject to federal limits on cost sharing and eligibility. that federal condition is central to the delay. medicaid is jointly administered by the states and the federal government, so new hampshire needs approval from the u.s. centers for medicare and medicaid services before the premium structure can operate. the bulletin reported that state officials have been weighing whether the planned premiums can coexist with h.r. 1 provisions that create cost sharing for some medicaid enrollees. the law’s cost-sharing provisions are scheduled to take effect in 2028, but the state is waiting for the federal government to clarify how the programs should be coordinated before it spends money to launch the collection system. a dhhs presentation to state lawmakers lists the conflict in its implementation timeline. the agency’s [medicaid changes from hr 1 document](https://gc.nh.gov/statstudcomm/committees/72/documents/medicaid%20changes%20from%20hr%201.pdf) says the state budget requires granite advantage premiums in state fiscal year 2027, while the federal cost-sharing requirement is scheduled for oct. 1, 2028. the same document says dhhs planned to submit a waiver by july 1, 2026; the current status reported by the department’s spokesperson shows that submission has not yet produced an approved launch path. the policy would affect more than a small administrative group. the [new hampshire fiscal policy institute](https://nhfpi.org/resource/the-state-budget-for-fiscal-years-2026-and-2027/) estimated that about 11,000 adults in granite advantage would be subject to the adult premiums. its review of the state budget said monthly charges would range from $60 to $100 depending on household size. the budget also includes a separate premium structure for households with children enrolled through the children’s health insurance program, with monthly amounts ranging from $190 to $270 for families above the applicable income threshold. supporters have described the premiums as a way to preserve broad eligibility while generating revenue for the program. opponents argue that even modest monthly charges can discourage enrollment or care, especially for people whose incomes sit just above the poverty line. a [new hampshire legislative analysis](https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/legacy/bs2016/hearingreport.aspx?id=11706&sy=2026) of a bill that would have repealed the premiums recorded both the planned july 1 start for medicaid expansion enrollees and the concern that the state could spend on a collection system that federal law may soon make obsolete. the bill was later listed as inexpedient to legislate and did not become the current governing law. for now, the practical answer for granite advantage members is that the new premiums have not started. the next major decision belongs to dhhs and federal medicaid officials: they must determine whether the state can secure approval, revise the design or wait for the federal cost-sharing framework. until that process produces a new authorization and timeline, new hampshire residents should not assume that the amounts listed in state law are current bills or that a launch date has been set. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord new hampshire new hampshire medicaid granite advantage health care costs dhhs federal approval public benefits

nh-public-colleges-tuition-waiver-promis.excerpt: The New Hampshire Promise will cover standard tuition for qualifying residents and community-college transfer students, but not every cost of attending college.
nh-public-colleges-tuition-waiver-promis.text: new hampshire public colleges to waive tuition for eligible students starting in 2027 the new hampshire promise will cover standard tuition for qualifying residents and community-college transfer students, but not every cost of attending college. new hampshire residents from families earning up to $100,000 a year will be eligible for tuition waivers at the state’s public universities and colleges beginning in fall 2027, under a new program announced by the university system of new hampshire. the program is aimed at incoming first-year students and certain community-college transfer students, opening another path into the state’s public higher-education system as families face rising college costs. the new hampshire promise covers standard tuition for eligible students at the university of new hampshire in durham and manchester, plymouth state university, keene state college and the university of new hampshire’s college of professional studies online program. the [official usnh program page](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) says the benefit is built from federal, state and institutional grant aid and applies to students who qualify for in-state residency. eligibility is narrower than the phrase ‘free college’ might suggest. students must be enrolled full time, pursuing a first undergraduate degree and meet the program’s academic and financial-aid requirements. usnh lists a minimum 2.7 grade-point average from a student’s prior school, submission of the free application for federal student aid and total family income of no more than $100,000 with typical assets. transfer students can qualify after earning an associate degree through the community college system of new hampshire. the program does not require a separate application. students must apply for admission to a participating usnh institution and complete the fafsa; the university system says eligible applicants will then be considered automatically as part of their financial-aid offer. awards will be reviewed annually based on the student’s fafsa, academic status and full-time enrollment, according to the system’s published guidance. that distinction matters for families planning a budget. the promise covers standard tuition, while students may still need loans or other aid for fees, books, housing and meals. the [university system of new hampshire’s eligibility guidance](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) also says the program does not apply to january or summer courses. the benefit is therefore a reduction of one major expense, not a guarantee that a student’s total cost of attendance will be zero. new hampshire public radio reported that the revised program is expected to broaden access compared with the previous version. tania deluzuriaga, a university of new hampshire spokesperson, told [nhpr](https://www.nhpr.org/education/2026-10-02/usnh-unh-plymouth-state-keene-state-tuition-waiver-higher-education-newhampshire) the system estimates 29% more of next year’s incoming class will qualify. under the earlier structure, students had to complete a more complicated federal pell grant process before learning whether they were eligible, a hurdle the new fafsa-based approach is intended to reduce. the announcement comes as new hampshire’s public colleges are managing financial pressure. nhpr reported that the system lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget and that unh cut $17.5 million from its budget, contributing to staff reductions and a hiring freeze while enrollment has also been declining. kimberly derego, the system’s chief enrollment officer, said the institutions will fund the waivers with endowment money and hope the program attracts donors who want to support lower-income students. for prospective students, the immediate next step is preparation rather than a new application deadline: watch the participating college’s admissions process, complete the fafsa for the relevant aid year and keep academic records current. the first cohort will not begin until fall 2027, and the system’s rules leave unanswered questions about how many students ultimately enroll, how the endowment-supported financing performs and whether the program changes enrollment patterns across the four campuses and online program. those results will determine whether the promise becomes a durable affordability tool for new hampshire families. new-hampshire nj-nuclear-task-force-2026-10-01.excerpt: The group’s first meeting created five subcommittees and a public information hub as New Jersey moves from lifting its nuclear moratorium toward planning new generation.
nj-nuclear-task-force-2026-10-01.text: new jersey nuclear task force maps next steps for 1,100-megawatt expansion the group’s first meeting created five subcommittees and a public information hub as new jersey moves from lifting its nuclear moratorium toward planning new generation. new jersey’s newly formed nuclear task force held its first meeting thursday, beginning a state effort to determine how next-generation nuclear power could fit into the state’s future electricity system. governor mikie sherrill’s office said the group reviewed a draft charter, created five subcommittees and launched nuclear nj, a public website for updates and background information. the meeting marks a shift from changing state policy to working out the practical questions that would come before a new reactor could be built. the administration says the task force is intended to coordinate work across government and with industry, labor, environmental groups and other stakeholders. it is not itself an approval for a plant, and the governor’s announcement did not identify a project site, developer or construction schedule. the five subcommittees divide that work into the areas most likely to shape any future proposal. one will examine regulatory and permitting requirements. others will study financing and power-sale arrangements, supply chains and technology, workforce development, and public trust. the last category is especially consequential for a technology that requires long-term safety oversight and community participation before construction could move forward. the task force has 14 members, according to its public roster. the group includes leaders from the governor’s office, the board of public utilities, the department of environmental protection, the economic development authority, the state treasurer’s office and the department of military affairs. it also includes representatives of pseg nuclear, holtec, the new jersey business and industry association, electrical workers, the laborers’ international union of north america and the natural resources defense council. that mix gives the panel access to industry and labor expertise, while also putting potential environmental and public-interest concerns inside the same planning process. the new group follows two major policy steps. sherrill’s executive order 2 established a nuclear power task force on her first day in office. in april, she signed legislation that ended new jersey’s roughly 50-year de facto moratorium on new nuclear development. the state later enacted the power nj act, which directs a competitive procurement program designed to support at least 1,100 megawatts of advanced nuclear generation. the bill describes that number as a program design parameter, not a guarantee that the state will ultimately buy that amount of power. new jersey already relies heavily on nuclear generation. the governor’s office says existing nuclear plants provide more than 40% of the state’s electricity and about 80% of its carbon-free power. supporters frame new reactors as a way to add reliable supply as electricity demand grows and to put downward pressure on utility costs. those are policy goals, not results that have been demonstrated by a new project; any cost, schedule, waste, safety and siting questions would have to be resolved through later regulatory and procurement decisions. independent reporting by new jersey 101.5 described thursday’s meeting as the start of planning for the 1,100-megawatt program and noted that the work is focused on permits, financing, workforce needs and public support. that account also underscored the distance between a planning target and operating power: the task force can organize the state’s next steps, but it cannot by itself make a reactor economical, secure federal approvals or settle questions about who bears construction risk. for residents, the immediate development is therefore an information and planning structure rather than a construction announcement. nuclear nj, developed with the board of public utilities, the economic development authority and the department of environmental protection, is intended to collect agency updates and explain the state’s approach. the next meaningful tests will be whether the subcommittees publish clear work products, how the state handles public input and whether any future procurement produces a proposal that can pass technical, financial, environmental and safety review. sources: [new jersey governor’s office](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/20261001b.shtml), [new jersey nuclear task force roster](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/about/task-force/), [new jersey department of environmental protection energy policy page](https://dep.nj.gov/cleanenergy/nj/), [new jersey 101.5 reporting](https://nj1015.com/new-jersey-nuclear-task-force-launches/), and [nuclear nj information hub](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/). more misc misc. nj trenton trenton, new jersey new jersey nuclear energy electricity power nj act energy policy

nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.excerpt: The state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals.
nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.text: new jersey opens health-benefits reform group as public-plan costs climb the state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals. new jersey has formally launched a working group to rethink the state health benefits program, putting labor, state officials, health-care organizations and public-employer representatives in the same process as the state begins its october enrollment season. the group is expected to produce advisory recommendations for gov. mikie sherrill on how to slow cost growth while preserving coverage for public employees, retirees and participating employers, according to the governor’s oct. 1 announcement (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20261001a.shtml). the launch fulfills a commitment in a sept. 2 agreement between the administration and 17 unions representing state employees. that agreement waived an increase in state workers’ health-benefit contribution rates for 2027 while giving labor a role in a broader review of the system. the state described the agreement as a response to structural cost pressures, not a final redesign of the plans. new jersey says its state, local-government and education health programs cover about 690,000 people combined (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260902b.shtml). the working group’s agenda reaches beyond the portion of premiums paid by employees. the governor’s office says members will examine how the state administers benefits, how insurers and providers are paid, the structure of provider networks, plan pricing, premium contributions, benefit design, participation rules, and the program’s governance and data systems. subcommittees will take up those subjects in more detail, and the administration says it may add outside experts and stakeholders as the review continues. that scope matters because new jersey’s public plans are not facing one uniform problem. state employees, local-government workers and school employees participate through programs with different plans, employers, governing bodies and legal requirements. independent reporting by the new jersey monitor found that a state commission approved an average 17.3% premium increase for local-government workers in september, while actuaries said the school employees’ plan needed an average 34.4% increase to fund claims, rebuild a month of surplus and repay a projected $90 million in state loans. the school-plan commission deadlocked, in part because one of its nine seats has been vacant (new jersey monitor: https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/09/03/nj-panels-ok-rate-hike-for-public-worker-health-plans-deadlock-on-increase-for-teachers/). the dispute is therefore tied to more than household payroll deductions. higher premiums can affect municipal budgets, school districts and the state’s cost of employing and retaining workers. the new jersey monitor reported that state actuaries estimated the state workers’ plan would need to collect $397.2 million more in 2027 premiums than in 2026, although that figure includes increases that otherwise would have been paid by the state and employees. the state’s earlier budget materials also projected roughly $6.7 billion in fiscal 2026 health-benefit payments for active and retired enrollees for whom the state is responsible (new jersey treasury: https://nj.gov/treasury/omb/publications/26bib/bib.pdf). the timing puts members and employers in a transition period. the state health benefits program’s open-enrollment window for the 2026 plan year runs from oct. 1 through oct. 31, while the school employees’ health benefits program’s enrollment period is scheduled for oct. 26 through oct. 31, according to the state treasury’s benefits page (new jersey department of the treasury: https://www.nj.gov/treasury/pensions/documents/hb/oe2026/hb-sbc-state-active-26.shtml). the reform group’s recommendations will not change those windows or immediately alter anyone’s plan. the group’s first meeting is scheduled for oct. 16. the administration says it will continue detailed design and implementation planning in 2027, and any resulting changes could require collective bargaining, administrative action, procurement steps, commission votes, legislation or other legal approvals. that means the immediate result is a process and a set of questions, not a promised savings figure or a new benefit package. the central test will be whether the review produces changes that address provider and prescription-drug costs while giving workers, employers and taxpayers clearer information about how the system is financed. more misc misc. nj trenton trenton, new jersey new jersey health benefits public employees labor health care costs

ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.excerpt: The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of New York households at risk.
ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.text: new york sues hud over housing-counseling funds as $1m state award hangs in balance the lawsuit challenges the trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of new york households at risk. new york attorney general letitia james sued the u.s. department of housing and urban development on wednesday, arguing that the agency unlawfully withheld federal housing-counseling money that supports homeowners, renters and prospective buyers across the state. the case was filed in the southern district of new york on the final day of the federal fiscal year, when the state said the underlying funds were scheduled to expire. the attorney general’s announcement is at https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-sues-trump-administration-protect-housing-counseling-0. new york is seeking to protect roughly $1 million it applied for through the new york state housing finance agency. the money would be distributed among 22 hud-certified counseling organizations, with individual grants historically ranging from $20,000 to $100,000. the programs provide guidance on home purchases, rent and mortgage finances, foreclosure prevention, property maintenance and other housing decisions. the state’s complaint says new york has received this federal support regularly for about 13 years and submitted a complete application on may 22, but never received an award or explanation from hud. the lawsuit challenges a broader funding decision. the complaint says congress made approximately $57.5 million available for hud’s national housing counseling program, but hud had not obligated at least $56.1 million by the time the case was filed. new york argues that federal law requires hud to make assistance available to approved housing agencies and that congress did not authorize the department to eliminate or reduce the program on its own. those are allegations in the state’s complaint, not findings by the court. the filing is available at https://ag.ny.gov/sites/default/files/court-filings/state-of-new-york-v-u.s-department-of-housing-and-urban-development-complaint-2026.pdf. the immediate dispute grew out of a september 25 announcement by president donald trump seeking to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal spending through a so-called pocket rescission. the associated press reported that the package included hud housing-counseling money along with other programs the administration criticized as unnecessary or ideologically driven: https://apnews.com/article/46b356590699e6225f783c74e7ee3597. in its complaint, new york says the administration’s public criticism focused on the perceived views of some grant recipients rather than the housing services the program funds. hud and the administration could contest that characterization in court. the potential impact is more concrete than the statewide grant total. new york’s attorney general says the state’s 2024 funding helped counseling organizations serve more than 7,000 households with one-on-one assistance, provide nearly 2,800 households with financial help to improve living conditions, prevent more than 250 evictions and nearly 300 foreclosures, and help almost 300 first-time buyers close on homes. those figures describe the prior year’s reported results; they do not establish how many households would lose services immediately if the 2026 grant is not restored. housing counseling is designed to help people navigate decisions that can determine whether they remain housed or can buy a home. hud’s current new york resource page directs residents facing foreclosure or seeking homeownership information to hud-approved counselors and related assistance: https://www.hud.gov/states/new-york?custom2=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f&og1=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f. that background helps explain why the funding fight reaches beyond nonprofit budgets: counselors can work with borrowers and tenants before a missed payment, foreclosure filing or failed purchase becomes harder to resolve. james is asking the court to declare hud’s actions unlawful, require the department to maintain the program and preserve the unobligated money while the case proceeds. the complaint also asks the court to prevent the funds from being transferred, returned to the treasury or otherwise made unavailable in a way that would frustrate relief. the filing does not itself restore the grants. the next significant step is a court decision on whether to preserve the money and require hud to act; until then, new york’s 22 counseling organizations and the households they serve face uncertainty over the state’s expected federal support. new-york nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.excerpt: The citywide Halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to Open Streets and plazas across all five boroughs.
nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.text: nyc plans record 160 car-free trick-or-streets locations for october the citywide halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to open streets and plazas across all five boroughs. new york city is expanding its trick-or-streets program to a record 160 car-free open streets and plazas this october, giving families in all five boroughs a month of halloween and fall events instead of a single-night celebration. the city says the locations will host trick-or-treating, face painting, live entertainment and games. the new york city department of transportation also plans to distribute about 75,000 pieces of candy. abc7 new york reported the same announcement wednesday, sept. 30, and described the program as the city's largest trick-or-streets event to date: https://abc7ny.com/post/mayor-mamdani-announces-nycs-largest-trick-streets-new-york/19892758/ the effort is designed around temporary changes to public space. community organizations, schools and cultural groups will turn selected streets and plazas into pedestrian-oriented gathering places, while the municipal art society of new york will offer free guided walking tours focused on neighborhood history, architecture and public spaces. street lab is also partnering with nyc dot and city schools on halloween-themed play and creative activities at selected school sites. five signature events anchor the schedule. brooklyn's hillel plaza celebration is set for oct. 22 from 2 to 6 p.m.; staten island's water street open street follows oct. 24 from noon to 5 p.m.; and queens' austin street open street is scheduled for oct. 25 from 2 to 7 p.m. manhattan's canal street open street and division plaza event is planned for oct. 28 from 3 to 7 p.m., while the bronx's james baldwin plaza event is scheduled for halloween, oct. 31, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. the department of transportation's event page lists additional neighborhood programs beginning oct. 3, including activities on vanderbilt avenue in brooklyn and castleton avenue on staten island. the calendar includes block parties, parades, dog events and school-linked programming throughout the month. nyc dot says individual events can be delayed or canceled because of weather, so families should check the official calendar before traveling: https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pedestrians/trickorstreets.shtml the month-long format matters because the program is also a test of how new york uses streets beyond their usual transportation role. the city's announcement says the participating groups will use the spaces for community celebrations and, in some cases, to support local foot traffic and neighborhood businesses. the setup gives organizers control over their own programming while the city coordinates the street closures and works with partner agencies. mayor zohran kwame mamdani and nyc dot commissioner mike flynn announced the expansion on sept. 30. this is the fifth year of trick-or-streets, according to nyc dot, which says the initiative is meant to add pedestrian space during one of the busiest periods for new york streets. the full map and schedule remain the best guide to what is happening on a particular block, because the 160 locations will not all be active at the same time. the primary announcement is available from the nyc mayor's office: https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/09/mayor-mamdani-announces-largest-ever-trick-or-streets-with-160-c new-york new-york new york ny new york new york ri-arts-climate-grants-2026-10-02.excerpt: The new program will fund artist-led projects that make climate information more accessible, with applications due Nov. 2 and work scheduled for 2027.
ri-arts-climate-grants-2026-10-02.text: rhode island opens arts-and-climate grants with $5,000 maximum award the new program will fund artist-led projects that make climate information more accessible, with applications due nov. 2 and work scheduled for 2027. rhode island artists and artist groups can now apply for a new grant program intended to turn climate information into public-facing art, stories and experiences. the rhode island state council on the arts, working with the executive climate change coordinating council advisory board, opened applications oct. 1 for the arts and climate grant. the application deadline is nov. 2 at 11:59 p.m., according to risca’s [grant guidelines](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate). the program is designed for projects that help residents understand climate change and participate in conversations about how communities should respond. risca says eligible work can address mitigation topics such as energy-efficient buildings, renewable energy, public transit, electric vehicles and heat pumps, or resilience issues such as flooding, extreme heat, stronger storms, sea-level rise, wetlands and community resilience hubs. the goal is not simply to decorate a climate campaign; the agency says artists may act as community connectors who gather local perspectives and carry those experiences back to state climate planners. awards can be as large as $5,000, although the grant page warns that partial awards are common. a partial award must be at least half of the request or $1,000, whichever is higher. the money is intended for projects taking place in rhode island between jan. 1 and dec. 30, 2027. risca expects to notify applicants in mid-december, with final reports due jan. 31, 2028. the first cycle is backed by $40,000 that the ec4 advisory board allocated to its partnership with risca from an $80,000 climate-communication award, according to the [program description](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate). the eligibility rules place the emphasis on rhode island residents working as the primary artistic force behind their projects. applicants must be at least 18, have lived in the state for at least one year and be legally resident in the united states with a tax identification number. groups of artists may apply, but the work must be artist-instigated and organized outside an institution’s formal program. projects may include a public performance, exhibition, curriculum, video, mural, brochure or other format, but risca says a pilot or public sharing is required when the proposal involves planning or curriculum development. the program’s structure reflects a practical problem in climate policy: technical plans can be difficult to understand even when they describe changes that affect daily life. rhode island’s climate agencies are working across issues that residents encounter locally, from coastal flooding and stormwater to home energy costs, transportation and heat. risca says projects should prioritize frontline communities, include community voices and use two-way engagement. that gives artists room to work at a neighborhood scale rather than requiring a statewide campaign or a large institutional production. the funding also comes with limits. grants cannot pay for capital construction or renovations, debt, regranting, prizes or events that are inaccessible to the public. applicants cannot use the program for work that is part of an undergraduate or graduate degree, and they cannot seek support for the same project through another risca grant, except for the agency’s general operating support for artists. awardees must credit risca and the ec4 advisory board in their marketing materials. risca will offer an online information session oct. 6 from 3 to 4 p.m. and another oct. 14 from 6 to 7 p.m., followed by drop-in support hours later in october and on the deadline day. the oct. 6 session will include an overview, a walkthrough of the application and time for questions, according to the [event listing](https://arts.ri.gov/events/arts-and-climate-grant-information-session). applications are submitted through risca’s online grant system. questions about the program can be sent to risca.contact@arts.ri.gov. the grant is administered by risca, but its climate-policy connection runs through ec4, the state council established under rhode island’s climate laws to coordinate mitigation and adaptation work. the [ec4 advisory board](https://climatechange.ri.gov/ri-executive-climate-change-coordinating-council-ec4/advisory-board) includes municipal representatives and members with expertise in economic policy, workforce development, natural and cultural resources, energy, education, public health and housing. the new grant therefore creates a small but concrete channel for residents’ creative work to inform the state’s broader resilience conversation. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri providence rhode island rhode island providence arts climate ri-route10-i95-ramp-closure-october-2026.excerpt: RIDOT will shut the Route 10 South ramp to I-95 North from 9 p.m. Friday until before Monday’s morning commute, then shift the ramp entrance as the Providence-Cranston interchange rebuild continues.
ri-route10-i95-ramp-closure-october-2026.text: rhode island route 10-to-i-95 ramp closes friday night for interchange work ridot will shut the route 10 south ramp to i-95 north from 9 p.m. friday until before monday’s morning commute, then shift the ramp entrance as the providence-cranston interchange rebuild continues. drivers heading from route 10 south to interstate 95 north at the providence-cranston line should expect a weekend detour beginning friday night. the rhode island department of transportation says the ramp will close at 9 p.m. on oct. 2 and reopen before the morning commute on monday, oct. 5, while crews connect a newly built bridge to the roadway leading toward i-95 north. the schedule remains subject to weather and construction conditions, according to ridot’s [i-95 15 project update](https://www.dot.ri.gov/projects/the-i-95-15/). ridot’s signed detour sends drivers onto the ramp for i-95 south, then off at exit 31c for jefferson boulevard. from there, motorists will turn left onto jefferson boulevard and left again to reach the northbound i-95 on-ramp. that route adds decisions and turning movements to a connection many commuters use to move between cranston, providence and the broader interstate network, so drivers who normally make the route 10-to-i-95 north move will need to watch for temporary signs and allow extra time. the closure is only one step in the traffic plan. on friday, before the nighttime shutdown, ridot expects to shift the beginning of the route 10 south-to-i-95 north ramp about 100 feet from its current position. drivers will enter the ramp sooner after the shift, while the nearby on-ramp to i-95 south will not change. once the northbound ramp reopens, motorists will be using the new alignment rather than returning to the present entrance. more changes are planned for mid-october at the route 1, or elmwood avenue, northbound ramp to route 10 north. ridot says drivers will have to choose a lane based on where they are going after the merge: the right lane for i-95 north, or the left lane for route 10 toward providence and exit 1c for i-95 south. the department plans additional signs and pavement markings, and says that arrangement will remain through spring 2027. the providence journal reported sept. 25 that the work is part of a larger effort to turn the route 10 segment between park avenue and the i-95 interchange into a boulevard-style connection. the newspaper said the planned design is intended to create a direct link between elmwood avenue and park avenue, with a shared-use bike path and improved pedestrian connections to roger williams park. that broader street design means the current ramp closures are tied to a long construction sequence, not a short resurfacing job. the scale of the corridor helps explain why a weekend ramp closure can affect more than the immediate interchange. ridot says the i-95 15 project corridor between providence and warwick carries about 185,000 vehicles each day, including roughly 9,000 trucks and other heavy freight vehicles. the agency also identifies hospitals, businesses and universities along the route, making reliable access important for commuters, deliveries and regional trips even when the affected ramp is only one part of the highway system. the project is designed to address 15 bridges rated poor or fair but nearing poor condition along i-95 and route 10. ridot lists providence, cranston and warwick as the project locations, a projected cost of $779 million and a construction schedule running from 2024 through 2031. the department says a $251 million federal bridge investment program grant helps offset the cost. it also says the work will remove three of rhode island’s five most-traveled structurally deficient bridges from that list. for friday-night travelers, the immediate issue is the route 10 south ramp closure and the signed jefferson boulevard detour. for regular commuters, the more lasting change will be learning the shifted entrance and the later lane assignments near elmwood avenue. ridot says construction schedules and traffic patterns can change with weather, project needs and field conditions, so drivers should check the department’s travel information and follow the signs in place when they approach the interchange. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri cranston ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: Fourteen districts and schools will use Rural Health Transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs.
ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.text: rhode island directs $5.48m to rural school healthcare career pathways fourteen districts and schools will use rural health transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs. rhode island is directing more than $5.48 million in federal rural health transformation program awards to 14 school districts and schools, creating or expanding healthcare career pathways in rural communities across the state. the rhode island department of education announced the awards wednesday at ponaganset high school in glocester. the department said the grants are designed to connect students with health careers in stages: career awareness in kindergarten through fifth grade, exploration in grades six through eight, and preparation for work or further study in grades nine through twelve. the announcement was also reported independently by [providence business news](https://pbn.com/foster-glocester-lands-largest-share-of-5-48m-rural-healthcare-cte-grants/). the money comes through the federal rural health transformation program, which is supported by the centers for medicare and medicaid services and the u.s. department of health and human services. rhode island says the broader program is intended to improve access to coordinated healthcare in rural communities. ride said its awards will reach the state’s 18 rural communities, while helping schools build relationships with healthcare providers and colleges. foster-glocester regional school district received the largest award, $1,360,343. the district plans to anchor its pathway at ponaganset with an on-campus physical therapy clinic, physical and occupational therapy programs, and a middle-school wellness initiative that introduces younger students to health careers. that design gives students a local setting to encounter the field before they have to choose a high school concentration or postsecondary program. other awards target distinct parts of the healthcare pipeline. burrillville schools received $928,574 for a biomedical sciences pathway and a new ems and health sciences learning center, with possible training in emergency medical services, nursing, phlebotomy, physical therapy and related fields. east greenwich public schools received $710,619 to launch what ride described as rhode island’s first pre-medicine career and technical education program, while modernizing learning spaces and adding work-based learning, medical simulation and ai-supported clinical tools. westerly public schools received $658,773 to improve its medical careers and ems pathway with simulation equipment, virtual-reality training, staffing and professional development. smithfield received $513,690 to expand biomedical sciences and add behavioral-health training. scituate received $318,191 to extend its biomedical pathway through the k-12 grades and add sports medicine, community health and emergency-response options. the remaining grants range from $25,604 for jamestown’s lawn school to $268,454 for narragansett high school, with projects also planned in
