ri-tiverton-pfas-water-line-grant-2026-1.excerpt: The USDA award will help the North Tiverton Fire District begin extending public water to households whose private wells exceed Rhode Island's PFAS standard, while testing and the source investigation continue.
ri-tiverton-pfas-water-line-grant-2026-1.text: tiverton secures $1m grant for water line after pfas well contamination the usda award will help the north tiverton fire district begin extending public water to households whose private wells exceed rhode island's pfas standard, while testing and the source investigation continue. tiverton has secured $1 million in federal assistance to begin extending public water service to homes whose private wells have been contaminated with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or pfas. the money is being provided through the u.s. department of agriculture's emergency community water assistance program to the north tiverton fire district, according to a sept. 29 announcement from the offices of u.s. sens. jack reed and sheldon whitehouse and rep. gabe amo. the grant is aimed at the crandall road, bulgarmarsh road and stafford road areas, where rhode island officials are continuing to test private wells. the lawmakers' announcement said more than 100 wells tested so far had exceeded rhode island's 20-parts-per-trillion standard, with some results above 4,000 parts per trillion. the lawmakers had backed the district's application in a sept. 8 letter to agriculture secretary brooke rollins, asking for emergency funding to restore reliable drinking water to affected homeowners. the award does not resolve the wider water problem. [what's up newp](https://whatsupnewp.com/2026/10/tiverton-gets-1-million-in-federal-funding-for-emergency-water-line-after-pfas-contamination/) reported oct. 1 that the grant will start the public-water extension, while testing and planning continue for other households. the publication said the town's effort is focused on homes with the most serious contamination first. a separate providence journal report, republished by [aol](https://www.aol.com/articles/help-coming-tiverton-homeowners-contaminated-185020000.html), said town officials were seeking to put the first section in the ground before winter and had sent the project out to bid, but the full buildout will require additional money and coordination. tiverton's [municipal pfas information page](https://www.tiverton.ri.gov/363/pfas-information) identifies the crandall road area as the subject of continuing investigation and posts updates from sept. 15, sept. 22 and sept. 28. the town cautions that its concentration map shows the known or suspected area of impact, not a property-by-property finding. it tells residents to rely on rhode island department of environmental management laboratory results and state guidance rather than assuming a home is safe or contaminated based only on its location. ridem says on its [emerging-contaminants program page](https://dem.ri.gov/ecsdc-grants) that it detected pfas above the state maximum contaminant level in a private well near crandall road and offered free testing to homes within a quarter-mile of the fire station or the initial detection. the agency says it is providing filtration systems at no cost to homeowners whose results exceed 20 parts per trillion. in its statewide emerging-contaminants program, dem says it is testing more than 800 private wells in 26 communities and using activated-carbon or reverse-osmosis systems where eligible results are above the state standard. the suspected source in tiverton has not been established. local reporting has noted the investigation's proximity to tiverton fire station 3 and the historical use of pfas-containing firefighting foam, but the state has not confirmed that the station caused the contamination. that distinction matters as officials decide whether public water, household treatment or other remedies are appropriate for each property. for residents, the immediate change is a path toward a permanent water connection for at least the first phase of the response, rather than continued reliance on bottled water or individual treatment while results arrive. the lawmakers said construction is expected to be completed before the end of december, though the schedule remains dependent on design, bidding, permits and the district's work. tiverton says it will continue posting test results, water-delivery information and public updates as the investigation develops. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri tiverton tiverton, rhode island rhode island tiverton pfas drinking water private wells usda grants environmental health

vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.excerpt: Applications will open Oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000.
vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.text: vermont to open $31.7m disaster-aid program for farms and timber businesses applications will open oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000. vermont will begin accepting applications oct. 26 for a $31.7 million disaster-recovery program aimed at farms, forest landowners and logging contractors that suffered qualifying weather-related losses in 2023 or 2024. the state says the first phase will cover up to 95% of an applicant’s eligible losses, with a maximum payment of $75,000. [gov. phil scott’s office](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-317-million-vermont-agriculture-timber-disaster) announced the program sept. 30 with the vermont agency of agriculture, food & markets and the department of forests, parks and recreation. the program is built from federal block-grant funding authorized under the american relief act of 2025. vermont’s [legislative joint fiscal office](https://www.ljfo.vermont.gov/grants-reports/) separately lists a $31,771,557 usda farm service agency grant for compensation tied to crop, timber and livestock losses, including on-farm infrastructure and weather damage. the aid is designed for businesses that are still operating and can document both the loss and its connection to an eligible weather event. the state says applicants may seek reimbursement for damage that has already been repaired, rebuilt or replanted, or may commit to completing eligible restoration or replanting with the funds. the program is non-competitive: applicants who demonstrate eligible, otherwise-unmet losses are intended to receive a payment, subject to the program’s rules and available documentation. for agricultural producers, eligible categories may include damage to on-farm infrastructure, bare-ground practices needed after a weather event, future economic loss and market loss. for the forest economy, the program can cover standing-timber and harvested-timber losses, licensed-forester assessment costs, updates to forest stewardship plans and certain recovery costs for loggers reopening damaged harvest sites. those categories reflect the different ways floods, hard freezes, excessive moisture and other severe weather can disrupt a farm or a logging operation beyond the cost of one immediate repair. the program follows years of recovery pressure from vermont’s storms and floods. independent reporting by [vtdigger](https://vtdigger.org/2026/06/10/feds-approve-31-7-million-in-disaster-aid-for-flood-hit-vermont-farmers/) described the federal award as specialized relief for farmers with limited access to other federal disaster programs, including people facing infrastructure and market losses from the 2023 and 2024 events. the state’s current notice expands the practical reach to timber landowners and contracted loggers as well as agricultural producers. applicants should begin assembling ownership, lease or timber-sale records; parcel information; tax or business identification; descriptions of the damage; dated photographs; receipts, invoices, repair records or estimates; and records of other payments for the same loss. timber applicants may also need stand maps, forest-management information, timber-sale records, revenue documentation and a licensed forester assessment for some claims. the state says the online application window is expected to close dec. 31, with payments anticipated in early 2027. the first phase is not the entire program. vermont says a second phase will address larger infrastructure projects valued above $75,000 and up to $750,000 through a competitive grant process. receiving a phase-one payment will not by itself bar an applicant from phase two, but the second phase cannot pay for losses already covered by phase one or another funding source. the outstanding questions for producers are how many businesses will apply, how much documented loss the program will face and how quickly the state can turn the october filing window into payments. new-england new-england new england vt montpelier vermont vermont agriculture timber disaster assistance flood recovery weather losses farm economy

vt-education-strategic-plan-2026-10-01.excerpt: The Agency of Education says the plan will guide work on college and career readiness, academic achievement, school climate and agency operations through 2030.
vt-education-strategic-plan-2026-10-01.text: vermont education agency unveils 2026-2030 plan built around four statewide priorities the agency of education says the plan will guide work on college and career readiness, academic achievement, school climate and agency operations through 2030. vermont’s agency of education has released a 2026-2030 strategic plan that sets a statewide direction for public education and lays out how the agency says it will measure progress. the plan was published oct. 1 after nearly two years of input from educators, students, families, school and district leaders and community partners, according to the [agency of education’s announcement](https://education.vermont.gov/press-release/vermont-agency-education-releases-statewide-strategic-plan) and a report by [vermont business magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/01/vermont-agency-education-releases-statewide-strategic-plan). the document arrives as vermont schools and state officials confront pressures that the agency identifies as declining enrollment, changing demographics, workforce strain and shifting expectations for graduates. those are statewide conditions rather than a promise that the plan will solve any one district’s budget or staffing problem. the agency describes its role as providing leadership, setting expectations, supporting schools and maintaining transparency and accountability for results. the plan organizes that work under four connected pillars. college and career readiness is intended to help students leave school with the knowledge, skills and experiences needed for what comes next. academic excellence for all focuses on teaching, meaningful learning and more equitable outcomes. safe and healthy schools covers the conditions that help students belong, engage and learn. operational effectiveness addresses the systems, data and capacity behind the agency’s work, according to the agency’s [strategic-plan webpage](https://education.vermont.gov/about/strategic-plan). the priorities are broad by design, but the agency says they will be translated into annual work. each year, officials plan to set priorities, identify milestones, measure progress and report on what they learn. the agency’s webpage also links to a 2026-27 implementation plan and a 2025-26 progress report, creating a structure for comparing the long-range goals with specific near-term actions. the plan’s development timeline shows how the agency assembled that framework. during a 2024 listen and learn tour, the agency says it heard from more than 1,000 education leaders, educators, parents, students and community members across vermont. in november 2025, it hosted more than 300 educators and other partners at a strategic-planning retreat. during 2026, participants from around the state met through steering committees to develop strategies tied to the agency’s vision. that process matters because the plan is not a new school-funding formula or a single mandate for local districts. it is an operating framework for the state agency, which oversees and supports vermont’s public education system while schools continue to make local decisions. its effect will depend on how the agency turns the four pillars into guidance, technical support, data reporting and decisions about where to direct its limited capacity. the agency’s announcement says the plan is meant to evolve as implementation produces new information. that gives the document a built-in review cycle, but it also leaves important questions for later reports: which student outcomes will be used as benchmarks, how milestones will be measured across districts with different circumstances, and whether the agency’s annual priorities match the needs heard during the public-input process. for now, the next step is the 2026-27 implementation plan and the reporting that follows it. vermont’s education agency says it will continue working with educators, families, students and community partners as the strategy moves from a published framework to yearly commitments. the plan’s value will ultimately be judged less by its four headings than by whether those commitments produce clearer support and better outcomes for students across the state. vermont education education vt vermont vermont education public schools education policy vt-teacher-apprenticeship-grant-2026-09-.excerpt: The new program will help educator-preparation providers build paid, debt-reducing routes to Vermont licensure, with applications due Feb. 23, 2027.
vt-teacher-apprenticeship-grant-2026-09-.text: vermont opens $300,000 grant path for teacher apprenticeships the new program will help educator-preparation providers build paid, debt-reducing routes to vermont licensure, with applications due feb. 23, 2027. vermont is making $300,000 available to expand teacher registered-apprenticeship programs, a new funding opportunity aimed at helping educator-preparation providers build debt-reducing routes into the profession. the [vermont agency of education](https://education.vermont.gov/news/grow-your-own-teacher-registered-apprenticeship-expansion-grant) announced the competitive subgrant sept. 29 with the vermont department of labor and the national center for grow your own, which will administer the application and award process. the grant is intended for programs that combine educator preparation with employment and supervised classroom experience. the agency of education says the opportunity is designed to create or expand teacher registered apprenticeship programs across the state, with particular attention to rural, high-need and underserved communities, including areas beyond vermont's current apprenticeship model. that focus matters in a state where recruiting and retaining licensed teachers is harder for small districts that compete across long distances and have fewer preparation options nearby. individual awards may reach $100,000 per distinct proposal. vermont-approved educator-preparation providers may lead an application, including approved colleges and universities and approved alternative-route providers that have a university or credit partner. out-of-state providers may participate as well. each proposal must include at least one vermont local education agency that will employ the apprentices and their assigned mentors, according to the agency of education's grant notice. the money is not a general scholarship pool for people who want to become teachers. it is intended to cover approved apprentice tuition, required fees and books for a complete pathway to initial vermont licensure. the state says grant funds and other available resources must ensure that selected apprentices pay nothing out of pocket for those costs. the arrangement can allow a school employee, such as a paraeducator, to earn while receiving training and moving toward a teaching license, although the grant notice does not promise a job or admission to any particular preparation program. the new round builds on a vermont apprenticeship system that has already tested teacher pathways. in its [2024 workforce report](https://legislature.vermont.gov/assets/legislative-reports/workforce-investment-system-registered-apprenticeship-program-annual-report-2024.pdf), the department of labor said a federal state apprenticeship expansion fund grant helped the vermont rural education collaborative work with school districts, the agency of education and other partners. that effort registered seven pre-k through grade 12 teacher-apprenticeship programs and had 28 apprentices in the program as of summer 2024. the same report said the agency of education had identified more than 1,300 teachers working on provisional or emergency licenses in april 2023, a dated measure of the staffing challenge rather than a current count. the prior model centered on vermont's northeast kingdom and used a hybrid structure: apprentices with bachelor's degrees in fields other than education worked under provisional or emergency licenses, received mentoring and completed online coursework and competency-based portfolios. the new grant is statewide and can support both new and existing programs, so its effect will depend on which providers apply and which districts are prepared to employ and mentor apprentices. prospective applicants can attend a pre-proposal conference oct. 7 from 2 to 3 p.m. eastern, with additional sessions scheduled for oct. 21, nov. 4 and jan. 13. applications are due feb. 23, 2027. the agency of education directs questions to the [national center for grow your own](https://ncgyo.org/vermont), whose grant page says the $300,000 allocation comes from an education grant to the organization from ascendium education group. the immediate next step is therefore planning: providers and districts must decide whether they can meet the partnership, licensure and no-out-of-pocket requirements before submitting a proposal. vermont education education vt vermont vermont education teacher apprenticeships teacher shortage registered apprenticeships rural schools vt-uvm-drink-spiking-investigation-2026-.excerpt: A Sept. 30 alert says the reports involve off-campus locations, a cash reward is available for information, and temporary weekend screening support will be offered to students in October.
vt-uvm-drink-spiking-investigation-2026-.text: uvm police investigate alleged drink-spiking reports in burlington a sept. 30 alert says the reports involve off-campus locations, a cash reward is available for information, and temporary weekend screening support will be offered to students in october. university of vermont police services is investigating reports that people may have been given incapacitating drugs without their knowledge at off-campus locations in burlington, prompting a campus safety alert and a request for information from students and the broader community. the sept. 30 alert says uvm police and safety teams received reports of alleged incapacitating or so-called date-rape drug incidents in the burlington area. it does not identify the locations, disclose what substances may have been involved or say how many people reported incidents. the alert says criminal investigations are ongoing and that uvm is offering a substantial cash reward for information that leads to the apprehension of a suspect or suspects. anyone with information is asked to call uvm police at 802-656-3473. ([uvm police alert](https://content.getrave.com/artifacts/api/v1/riki/alert/2645895/moreinfofile/3e2e5059-d183-4ba2-a0d6-d4fc2bc6acd8)) local reporting adds limited context but does not resolve those unknowns. [wcax reported](https://www.wcax.com/2026/09/30/uvm-police-warn-drink-spiking-offer-reward-information/) that sources described three or four incidents at different locations. [wptz reported](https://www.mynbc5.com/article/uvm-police-investigate-alleged-date-rape-drug-incidents/73967944), citing uvm chief safety and compliance officer michael schirling, that officials believed the reports involved multiple distinct events, multiple people and more than one location. those descriptions are part of an active investigation, not a court finding that a crime occurred in any particular case. burlington police told wcax they had not seen a trend of these incidents. that distinction matters: uvm’s alert is a warning about allegations under investigation, not a declaration that a citywide pattern has been established. the reports also concern off-campus places, so the alert reaches beyond the university’s property and asks anyone who may have information to come forward. uvm urged people attending parties or visiting bars and restaurants to avoid leaving drinks unattended, reject open drinks from others and seek help quickly if they feel suddenly weak, confused or otherwise unwell. uvm’s existing [incapacitating-drug screening initiative](https://www.uvm.edu/dsc/incapacitating-drug-screening-initiative), operated with uvm medical center, is designed for students who believe they were drugged but do not necessarily suspect a sexual assault. the university says testing is most useful when obtained promptly because some substances leave the body quickly. the program says student health services can provide screening, and that testing may be tracked anonymously on request. if sexual assault is suspected, uvm directs people to the uvm medical center emergency department for examination and treatment. the new alert adds a short-term change for october: weekend on-call support will be available for screening, giving students an option besides going directly to an emergency department. uvm says students can contact police services and be connected with a student health services medical provider through the center for health and well being. the university also says reporting does not force a person into a full investigation; its screening guidance describes options ranging from a full report to sharing only basic timing and location information that may help investigators identify patterns. the next steps are investigative. uvm police are seeking tips, but the alert does not announce an arrest, identify a suspect or establish whether the allegations are connected. students and community members who feel unsafe or witness a crime in progress should call 911; people seeking confidential support can contact hope works, which uvm lists as a 24-hour resource at 802-863-1236. until investigators release more information, the confirmed public facts are the alert, the request for tips and the temporary screening support—not a confirmed count of victims or a proven explanation for what happened. new-england new-england new england vt burlington burlington, vermont vermont burlington university of vermont vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.excerpt: Five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the Vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer.
vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.text: federal charges widen legal fight over williston ice facility protests five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer. federal prosecutors have charged five people accused of repeatedly blocking access to an immigration and customs enforcement facility in williston, opening a new legal track in a protest campaign that has already produced separate state trespass cases. the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of vermont said sept. 30 that peter booth, 58, of jericho; lexington kennedy, 22, of new york city; henry prensky, 80, of burlington; roan wade, 23, of red hook, new york; and sherri wormser, 57, of colchester were charged by information with obstructing access to the ice national criminal analysis and targeting center. the facility is in the white cap business park in williston, according to the [department of justice announcement](https://www.justice.gov/usao-vt/pr/five-people-charged-obstructing-access-federal-facility-williston-vermont). the allegations involve three protest dates. prosecutors say all five entered the building’s atrium on feb. 9 and used their bodies to block doors leading to the federal facility after warnings to disperse. the justice department says booth and prensky did so again on may 14, while kennedy and wade repeated the conduct on july 24. in each instance, the release says, access was restored after law enforcement removed protesters from the building. the federal case is narrower than a general challenge to protest activity: the charging document alleges obstruction of entrances and exits, not simply opposition to immigration policy. first assistant u.s. attorney jonathan ophardt said the blockades created safety risks for people working at the facility and required a substantial police response. those are the government’s allegations, not findings by a court. the defendants have not yet been scheduled for initial appearances. the justice department said each faces up to 30 days in prison and a fine of up to $5,000 if convicted, with any sentence to be set by the court under the applicable factors. the agency also said the five had not retained or been appointed counsel when the announcement was issued. all five are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. the charges add to a separate vermont prosecution arising from a july 24 demonstration at the same office complex. vermont attorney general charity clark filed unlawful-trespass cases against 13 people arrested during that sit-in; twelve pleaded not guilty at a sept. 24 arraignment, and the case of an 18-year-old was transferred to family court. [vermont public’s reporting](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-09-24/vermont-attorney-general-charges-protesters-for-trespassing-at-ice-surveillance-facility) said the state charge carries a maximum of three months in prison, a $500 fine, or both. vermont public reported oct. 1 that three of the five people named in the federal case also face state charges. the outlet described the federal action as an escalation after chittenden county state’s attorney sarah george previously declined to prosecute some protesters arrested during sit-ins, while clark’s office later took up the july cases. that split has made charging decisions part of the local debate over how vermont should respond to civil disobedience at the facility. for williston, the immediate issue is practical as well as legal. the white cap complex has become a recurring site of demonstrations, arrests and competing claims about public safety, federal immigration enforcement and protest rights. the next concrete step in the federal matter is the defendants’ initial court appearance; until then, the charging information establishes what prosecutors allege but does not resolve whether the conduct violated federal law or how the cases will affect future demonstrations. new-england new-england new england vt williston williston, vermont vermont williston immigration enforcement protests federal courts public safety
